Furthermore, we explored potential impacts on other rare $B^0_s$ decays. Our study finds the upper limit on the lifetime of this specific decay mode, which could pose a threat to the flavor-changing-neutral-current discrepancy between QCD and SM or even indicate the presence of a long-lived axion-like particle. To further investigate this anomaly, we suggest enhancing the precision in measuring $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ and other similar decays. Our analysis indicates that a significant improvement in measurement accuracy could be achieved with around 100 times more data at LHCb's current energy level, allowing for a more detailed examination of this potential anomaly in the future. Additionally, with the advent of HL-LHC, a notable enhancement in sensitivity is anticipated, which could potentially validate our findings. To that end, we propose the designation of a more distinctive name for this specific decay mode in the upcoming HL-LHC benchmark processes. This paper builds upon our previous work in [1], specifically focusing on quantum dynamical systems whose underlying algebra is a Lie algebra. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between the deformed Fock space and the algebraic sum of oscillators, and we express the Hamiltonian of the system in terms of the basis functions. Additionally, we determine the conditions under which the systems exhibit unitary evolution, and we derive the closed form of the time-evolved wave function. We based our analysis on the Dunkl operator approach, and we demonstrate the compatibility of our results with the Lie algebra approach. We also discuss the applicability of our results to multiple particle systems, and we highlight the simplicity of our time-evolution formula in comparison to the standard method. We examine our results for the $su(2)$ algebra, and we provide an analytical example of a time-dependent system, and we show how the unitary evolution condition can be satisfied. We conclude by discussing the scope of our research, and we explore the potential connection between our work and superintegrable systems. We ended with an interesting open question related to our findings. We refer to our previous work [1] for the definition of quantum dynamical systems, their underlying algebra, and the Dunkl operator approach. However, we do note that in [1], we defined the algebra as a commutative algebra, and with this paper, we intentionally relax this assumption to investigate noncommutative quantum dynamical systems. We trust that this paper will contribute meaningfully to the study of noncommutative quantum dynamical systems. We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring, demosaicking, and denoising raw images by learning a single image processing pipeline that can handle the blurring, mosaic pattern, and noise affecting the images. Our primary goal is to train a collaborative process that can deal with these effects simultaneously. To achieve this, we develop a new mathematical model that represents the relationships between the raw images, blurring, mosaic pattern, and noise. This model enables us to utilize a single optimization problem to solve the entire image processing task. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative raw image processing pipeline that can be efficiently trained using deep learning techniques, specifically supervised convolutional neural networks. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted several experiments demonstrating its superiority over traditional and state-of-the-art deep learning methods in raw images. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhmzhmzh/CD3. Additionally, we provide an over-scanned camera blurring simulation model that outperforms existing simulation models, also making it open-source. Our technique holds potential applications in enhancing low-quality camera systems and recovering detailed raw images from processed images. To take it a step further, we explored demosaicking as a separate process but still utilized a collaborative approach, referring to it as CD1, and found it to be a challenging problem, especially with weak demosaicking cues. On the other hand, we discovered that incorporating additional cues, specifically the demosaicking process, facilitates collaborative raw image processing, resulting in improved outcomes, which we termed CD2. All models discussed in this paper have been incorporated into a modular framework accessible here: https://github.com/zhmzhmzh/CD3/tree/main/demo/CD2_group. With these patterns, models trained in an end-to-end fashion using raw images achieved better deblurring results than those trained on processed images. In this talk, we revisit Dirac's Formula from the Minkowski Spacetime perspective. We then examine what happens to this formula when the Minkowski Spacetime is replaced with an $R$-Minkowski Spacetime. We provide an alternative proof of the modified Dirac's Formula proposed by B. T. Chan and J. A. Hickey, offering a comparison with their approach. We also offer a new perspective on the conformal symmetry of the Dirac operator when operating on functions in $R$-Minkowski Spacetimes. Finally, we explore potential applications of the modified Dirac's Formula to harmonic functions within these spacetimes. We also investigate the relationship between the $R$-Minkowski Spacetime Laplacian and the Dirac operator itself, establishing a connection that may be useful in future research. We conclude by outlining several open questions and potential areas for further investigation.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles of bivectors within this framework, starting from their basic definitions and moving on to detailed calculations, ultimately showing how they help in determining the conformal metric of Weyl curvature. It also explores the relationship between bivectors and the complex self-dual fields in Riemannian geometry. The Newman-Khan metric, previously posted on arXiv, is rederived as an example of a bivector-based calculation. The paper also examines how these bivectors can be utilized to find the Weyl curvature conformal metric in various scenarios, including when the complex self-dual field is directly provided and when it needs to be derived from the Klein-Gordon field. It demonstrates the bivector-based approach by explicitly calculating the Weyl curvature conformal metric for the Newman-Khan metric. The general bivector-based framework is then applied to several well-known metrics, including the Kerr metric, leading to a new, bivector-based interpretation of this metric. The paper also addresses an issue related to flat bivectors and presents an alternative, more direct path to determining the conformal metric of Weyl curvature, bypassing the need for flat bivector analysis. It is now accessible on arXiv at the following link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.00431. This count is already known to equal the sum of two numbers - the counts of bitangents that can be paired with a sign, and the counts of bitangents that can't. We use a combination of classical and modern techniques to show that the former is half of the total, and the latter is three-quarters of the total. We also offer an elementary $\mathbb{A}^1$-version of this result. For quartic surface doubles with four nodes, we show that the bitangents that can't be paired come in two distinct types - those that are tangent to a third node, and those that aren't. The former has a count of 19800, the latter has a count of 7884. The former type of bitangents can be paired with the same method used for bitangents to a plane quartic. The latter type of bitangents can be paired by applying a sign to each of the 13200 four-node configurations that project to a bitangent, with an additional 5564 such configurations that are tangent to a third node. These additional configurations account for the fact that some bitangents can be paired in more than one way. The 13200 figure of four-node configurations that project to a bitangent also answers a question posed by F. Kiraly. Tantalum oxide (Ta$_2$O$_5$) is an insulating material with oxygen vacancies that significantly affect its electronic properties. To understand Ta$_2$O$_5$, it is necessary to characterize the concentrations of vacancies in this material. A recent study used a combination of first-principles simulations, Monte Carlo simulations, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to determine the average oxygen coverage on Ta$_2$O$_5$ substrates. However, there is some discrepancy in the results, leading to different interpretations of how oxygen coverage affects the local geometry of Ta atoms. One view suggests that higher oxygen coverage (up to 5 atoms) leads to a higher energy state in Ta 4d bands, whereas the other perspective indicates that this increase in energy occurs when there are fewer oxygen atoms around Ta, providing a conflicting explanation for the experimental findings. To resolve this difference, additional Monte Carlo simulations with consideration of point defects are carried out, ultimately providing a clearer understanding of how oxygen coverage affects the local geometry of Ta atoms and the Ta 4d bands, as supported by experimental data. Furthermore, a model that incorporates many-body effects is proposed to describe the Ta 4d bands, offering a framework that could be applied to other transition metal oxides. Additionally, by comparing different supercells used to model Ta$_2$O$_5$, it is demonstrated that a larger unit cell is more suitable for capturing the electronic properties of this material. Lastly, to facilitate further investigation, all computational models employed in this study have been made available for public access. Moreover, the results obtained from the simulations can be compared to experimental techniques such as X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) to better understand the properties of Ta atoms in this material. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive insight that could be applied to other materials with similar point defects, ultimately key to understanding their electronic properties. Therefore, it is essential to consider not only the concentration of vacancies but also their spatial distribution and how it affects the local geometry of atoms within these materials. X-ray binary observers face a challenge: tracking suspicious activity in real-time stream data containing numerous events from various sources. Current methods are ineffective for dealing with large volumes of data and need significant human input to adjust their rules. This paper introduces a novel approach called DOVE, focused on detecting unusual activity patterns in real-time data streams from X-ray binaries using their past behavior as a guide. DOVE uses a linear regression model to forecast typical activity levels, combining this with an anomaly detection method to identify and mark periods of abnormal activity. This landmark article summarizes DOVE's development; further details on its implementation, performance on historical binary data, and its potential for addressing other rapid astrophysics surveillance issues are provided in the accompanying paper available at https://github.com/ebertjr/dove-documentation.

Teaching robots via demonstration relies on the capacity to decode and replicate the actions' underlying physics. In contrast to solely action-based learning, our research supplements robotic training with a learning-to-interpret component that analyzes instructor audio feedback when demonstrating physical manipulations. Our primary objective is to demonstrate the potential benefits of combining audio and action data for robotic learning. When presented with both auditory and visual information, we find that speech recognition and semantic analysis enhance robotic performance when replicating demonstrated tasks. Furthermore, we identify specific auditory features that contribute to decoding the underlying physics of the demonstrated tasks. When speech and action data disagree, we develop a strategy to select the more reliable source, based on the features identified, which results in improved robotic replication of complex manipulations. Our research provides insight into the relationship between acoustic patterns and instructed robotic learning, paving the way for the exploration of speech's role in teaching robots via demonstration. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation framework that assesses robotic generalization of physical concepts from audio-visual instruction. In line with the established evaluation protocols, we conduct a series of user studies with human instructors to demonstrate the method's applicability and the benefits of combining audio and action data. When compared to action-based learning, our results show a statistically significant improvement (p < 10^-3) when robots are trained with acoustic patterns and demonstrate a mean 20% reduction in errors when replicating complex manipulations. When speech and action data are mismatched, our approach results in a 15% decrease in errors (p < 10^-2) and outperforms all control conditions in our user studies. Our research may offer valuable insights for the development of more effective human-robot interaction interfaces, critical for creating robots that can excel in various tasks with the guidance of humans. In order to succeed in various manipulation tasks, robots need to be able to decode the underlying physics of the objects they are instructed to manipulate. When demonstrating how to perform a task, humans supply both auditory and visual information to the robot. Although speech and action data provide the robot with a more comprehensive understanding of the demonstration, it has been observed that the auditory feedback given by humans during demonstrations contains valuable information that can enhance the robot's replication of the demonstrated task. When speech and action data disagree, the robot should select the more reliable source, based on the features identified, which results in the robot replicating the demonstrated task more accurately. This research provides insight into the relationship between acoustic patterns and instructed robotic learning, paving the way for the exploration of speech's role in teaching

While automated quality assessment techniques are widely employed in other imaging technologies, such as X-ray computed tomography and ultrasound, there are unique challenges associated with medical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). For instance, poorly acquired MRI data can still produce high-quality images if appropriate reconstruction techniques are applied, which complicates the development of an automated quality assessment tool. Furthermore, training and evaluating such a system are crucial steps in its development. However, existing evaluation methods prioritize classification performance over the intricate nuances of MRI quality, which involves assessing multiple dimensions including spatial consistency, tissue contrast, and noise levels. This paper highlights the intricate nature of MRI quality, which cannot be captured by a single classification label, and emphasizes the necessity of incorporating all relevant quality aspects in the training of a quality assessment algorithm. To achieve this, we developed a comprehensive training regimen that utilizes a designed set of multi-dimensional anchors which cover the quality spectrum in all relevant dimensions. Our results demonstrate the significant improvement in both classification accuracy and system robustness achieved with this approach, resulting in a more capable and adaptable quality assessment algorithm. Our research provides a solid foundation for the further development of automated MRI quality assessment tools. By combining a hierarchical taxonomy from the Wikipedia category network, TopicCenter effectively filters out irrelevant entities and reduces redundancy by incorporating a minimal set of entities connected to the topic's central node. Our experiments demonstrate that TopicCenter's unique layered diagram component offers distinct benefits, and when integrated into the Yahoo! Knowledge Network, it excels in entity suggestion performance compared to established methods. Furthermore, TopicCenter shows potential in entity grouping tasks. Our approach, specifically the layered diagram approach, is made available for others to use through an open-source repository. Overall, TopicCenter represents an enhanced framework for entity suggestion, particularly in complex knowledge graphs like Wikidata. To complement TopicCenter's entity suggestion capabilities, we introduce a publicly accessible entity suggestion dataset that incorporates human feedback, along with a detailed analysis of the dataset's characteristics. Our study indicates that existing entity representation models, although highly effective in various tasks, struggle to prioritize important entities related to a specific topic. In contrast, TopicCenter, with its layered diagram approach, successfully recommends a diverse and relevant entity set that excels in internal and external evaluation criteria. In terms of scalability, our approach is suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs, as evidenced by its performance on the Wikidata knowledge graph. To facilitate deeper understanding of TopicCenter's entity suggestion focus, we conduct a thorough visualization of the layered diagram, making it clear that the approach's effectiveness relies on the unique combination of the Wikipedia category hierarchy and minimal connectivity. Our exploration of TopicCenter's parameter influence, along with its robustness results, provide valuable insights, as they indicate a close relationship between the topic's central node degree and suggested entities' relevance. Collectively, our results and the accompanying supplementary materials offer a comprehensive TopicCenter overview, complete with a discussion on potential future directions. With its exceptional performance, versatility, and clear code, TopicCenter is an exceptional choice for entity suggestion tasks, as well as a valuable resource for the broader research community. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the standard Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold. Building upon this, we also prove that a trivial steady Cotton soliton occurs under the condition that the Reeb vector field's eigenvalue of the Ricci operator is non-negative. Moreover, we prove that a shrinkage-type Cotton soliton cannot exist on nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Finally, we demonstrate the incompatibility of a conformal Killing vector field with an eigenvalue of the Ricci operator on these manifolds. Based on the above findings, we establish that a non-trivial steady Cotton soliton with an incompressible distribution can not exist on nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Reinforcement learning experiences difficulties when applied to tasks that involve exploring a vast state space with multiple dynamics, resulting in slow policy updates. An widely accepted approach to overcome this challenge is the use of sampling methods that prioritize data with significant value differences. Despite its effectiveness, the traditional method of exploiting the most varied data has several limitations, primarily because it relies heavily on the initial samples, resulting in inefficient discovery of states that represent a mix of the current policy's strengths and weaknesses. To address this shortcoming, we propose a new form of experience replay that selectively selects data with low variance, allowing for the update of the policy in an online setting. The proposed method is compared to existing replay methods, resulting in notable improvements, especially in domains that involve multiple state and action variables. The proposed method is a practical solution to the challenge of updating policies in a changing environment, with potential applications in topics such as transfer learning and robust policy updates. I'd like to introduce libcommute, a cutting-edge C++11/14/17 and Python 3.8+ toolkit that uses the libcommute C++11/14/17 NTL-based wrapper to efficiently manage polynomial representations of the generators of the U(N) Lie algebra. Specifically, libcommute utilizes the Fock basis to define a set of commuting operators commonly employed in many applications, including exactly one of each: number operator, creation operator, annihilation operator, density matrix, or two distinct interaction operators. The program's central functionality enables the conversion of these operators to the standard second quantization form and subsequently computes the exact diagonalization results for any given state. The libcommute library also provides the capability to automate the creation of these polynomial representations, eliminating the need for the libcommute specification language. The language's automated features are complemented by various tools, including a graphical user interface and the libcommute specification parser in Python, making it an all-encompassing toolkit for managing the program's underlying data structures and fundamental operations. The libcommute C++11/14/17 code is distributed under the permissive BSD 3-Clause License. The Python 3.8+ version of the program is offered as part of the pycommute package on the PyPI package repository. The documentation for the C++11/14/17 and Python 3.8+ versions, along with example use cases and the libcommute specification language guidelines, are available at https://libcommute.github.io/. The program is the result of significant contributions from multiple authors, as detailed in the contributors list. The libcommute project was conceived by R. Eder and thoroughly supervised by J. McIver. The program is free for any type of usage, including commercial purposes, requiring only that users acknowledge its source in their publications by referencing arXiv:1808.04516. The program's design is influenced by the ideas presented in the seminal work arXiv:1707.08101. The libcommute-based research presented in these proceedings focuses on the interplay between unitary evolution, mutual interaction, and initial conditions, with particular attention on the emergence of non-equilibrium states. These proceedings are supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, with the libcommute toolkit also being openly available for any future research projects. Notably, when we focus on the surface layer, our findings coincide with previous research on (Ba0.6K0.4)Fe2As2 that included voids. This textural distribution is thought to originate from differences in growth rates between the (Ba0.6K0.4)Fe2As2 crystals and the underlying substrate during synthesis. This particular superconductor's electronic architecture is influenced by both its crystal structure and the presence of voids. Our study discovered a close relationship between these voids and the superconductor's superconducting properties, particularly in the (Ba0.6K0.4)Fe2As2 material without voids. However, when voids are present, as seen in our textured data, there are significant alterations in the superconductor's electronic properties, leading to a decrease in the superconducting transition temperature. This change raises interesting implications regarding how to enhance a material's superconducting properties when that material can form voids during synthesis.

Recently introduced, the superbosonization formula by Odashima and Sato provides a useful transformation for converting Gaussian boson models into equivalent free-fermion models. This study investigates the relationship between the superbosonization formula and an established method by Sato, which employs the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to achieve the same goal. Our analysis reveals that the two approaches are equivalent and demonstrates the utility of the superbosonization formula by rederiving popular applications of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. Furthermore, this study shows that the superbosonization formula offers a more efficient and simpler path to developing Gaussian boson models with long-range interactions. This advancement is particularly valuable for models whose symmetry group cannot be readily identified, making it more challenging to apply the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. As a result of this study, several new family members of SU(Nc) Gaussian boson models with long-range interactions can be constructed using the superbosonization formula. These models encompass both compact and non-compact versions, as well as cases with zero and non-zero chemical potentials. This class of models can also be represented using a superfermion representation, obtained through the application of the superbosonization formula to a specific set of superfermion lattice models. This connection reveals that certain SU(Nc) boson models can be viewed as superfermion models with multiple species. This interpretation provides a new perspective on previous research, revealing that certain compact models are equivalent to a class of non-compact models parameterized by the superfluid density. This relationship holds for any Nc, indicating that any given SU(Nc) boson model can be converted into a corresponding superfermion model, and vice versa. This advancement enables the direct application of superfluid density as an model parameter, offering a clearer understanding of boson models with this parameter. Despite the intricate nature of these theories, the theories themselves must be tangible, reflecting the underlying reality that the world is composed of.  In this context, I would like to explore the intersection of particle physics and cosmology, focusing on dark matter - a mysterious phenomenon affecting the universe's evolution, yet inexplicable in the absence of a governing force.  Our primary tool for investigating this phenomenon is the Large Hadron Collider, which has given us a powerful tool to do so.  However, in order to fully utilize this tool, we must consider the smallest of particles that make up matter and the forces that act upon it, as well as the most basic characteristics that any particle physics theory must possess.  At the heart of this lies the universality of the gravitational force, which arises from the intersection of space and time, requiring a minimum of two particles with appropriate properties to interact with each other.  This knowledge serves as the foundation for our search for dark matter, which involves looking for evidence of the presence of these two-particle interactions, as well as the interaction of matter particles with each other, with themselves, and with the Higgs boson, which gives matter its mass.  Furthermore, I will examine the current state of our knowledge about dark matter, which is largely based on the properties of only a single particle - the quark, specifically the up and down variants - and I will explore the numerous particle candidates that have been proposed to constitute dark matter, many of which can be formed from the combination of multiple quarks, as well as other combinations of particles. Changing lanes is a common technique used by drivers to maneuver to a different road section, but it's also a maneuver that poses significant risks if not executed properly. Given the automated nature of driving systems, it's crucial for their reliability that they can accurately predict a vehicle's actions while changing lanes. Current deep learning models used for action recognition often require lengthy video segments as input, but they may not always perform well with shorter segments, particularly if the model is not optimized for such cases. This research aims to enhance the detection of hazardous actions, specifically lane change crashes, by training a deep learning network on a dataset of brief video clips featuring vehicles changing lanes. To facilitate faster and more precise detection, the network is designed to utilize a segmentation mask to focus on the vehicle's movement over time. With support from extended IoU-based segmentation masks, the proposed system demonstrates superior performance over conventional deep learning architectures, as evident from its high accuracy rates and minimal false negatives in detecting hazardous lane change actions. Experimental results show that the new deep learning architecture, combining a spatiotemporal network with segmentation mask transfer, achieves notable improvements in lane change crash detection, especially when comparing its performance to that of a baseline model using a similar but distinct network. Furthermore, the research introduces an innovative mask extension technique, called Super Mask, which allows for faster feature extraction by incorporating a subset of the more complex VGGNet layers. As a result, the team was able to successfully integrate the high-performance deep learning network on an autonomous driving platform, showcasing its capability to identify lane change crashes through real-world demonstrations. With its outstanding performance and ability to operate on actual vehicles, the system represents a ground-breaking achievement in the field of autonomous driving. However, it's essential to note that creating a fully reliable and precision-oriented system for detecting hazardous lane change crashes necessarily requires collecting a comprehensive and varied dataset of video clips, as well as thoroughly testing the system on real-world data to ensure its effectiveness and robustness. Nevertheless, the proposed deep learning architecture, along with its innovative mask extension technique, provides a promising direction for future research in the field of action recognition and autonomous driving. Although introducing a fully-fledged temporal transfer network along with an extended mask set yields promising results in detecting lane change crashes, it presents difficulties in implementing similar temporal transfer learning on actual driving scenarios due to its complex design. Therefore, the team suggests a more manageable approach, incorporating a straightforward deep learning architecture along with a simple mask extension, as a more suitable solution for a wide range of driving activity recognition. The occurrence of stable oscillations in rotating stars has been widely accepted for several decades, however its theoretical applications are still limited. To make progress in this field, we developed a cutting-edge numerical approach to model stars in rotation, utilizing a one-dimensional grid of computational cells. By implementing this approach in the EVOL code, we successfully simulated rotating stars for both main sequence and massive stars in binary systems, and our algorithm was recently incorporated into the COMPUTSTAR compact objects models. In the present study, we further developed the approach to handle stars with external heat sources and massive objects experiencing mass loss. To validate our method, we simulated numerous scenarios, including constant external heating, radiative acceleration, wind loss, supernovae explosions, and massive losses, without any notable deviations from expected outcomes. Our approach has the benefit of generating precise equations of state, which has the advantage of allowing post-processing tools to analyze oscillations, convection, and other stellar phenomena in a more realistic manner. To facilitate the use of our approach in computational astrophysics, we have made our code publicly available. By providing access to our code, we aim to facilitate the exploration of oscillations in stars across the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, ultimately contributing to a deeper comprehension of stellar physics. To this end, we have created an interactive tool that combines our code with Matthew Breitzer's EVOL code visualization features, allowing users to visualize convective patterns, oscillations, and the effects of external heating on stars. To further expand our research, we have made the code available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/mbreitzer/evol_code, where users can find the code that combines our approach with the EVOL code, along with any further developments made to it. Additionally, we have issued a Call to Action to computational astrophysics researchers to utilize our approach in their research involving oscillations in stars, and to share their results on the GitHub repository mentioned above. By doing so, we aim to create a comprehensive collection of studies using our approach, while also facilitating the exchange of ideas and expertise among researchers in this field. To better comprehend the detection challenges associated with oscillations in stars, we have established a working framework that combines our approach with Matthew Breitzer's EVOL code visualization features, allowing us to analyze the effects of external heating on oscillations in stars. This framework, along with the code that combines our approach with the EVOL code, has been made available on the GitHub repository mentioned above, where users can find any further developments

Specifically, we determined the resonance energies as a function of temperature, using the full band structure instead of just the $d$-projected one. Our findings show that the $d$ resonance energies vary between 1.5 and 3.5 eV, and display only a slight temperature dependence. The $s$ resonance energies, however, drop from around 2 eV at high temperatures to around 1 eV at lower temperatures. These results have significant implications for the choice of model parameters in the impurity model, particularly in the correlation values and the residual hybridizations. We found that the residual $p$-$d$ hybridizations play a crucial role in understanding the results obtained from the impurity model, and that they are temperature dependent, with the $s$-$d$ hybridizations displaying an even more pronounced temperature dependence. If these results are incorporated into the impurity model, the obtained spectral functions show a better match with the experiments, with the inclusion of the $s$-$d$ hybridizations yielding a more accurate representation of the experimental data. Furthermore, we observed that the $s$-$d$ hybridizations cause the spectral weight to shift from the $s$-like orbital to the $d$-like orbital as the energy increases, with this effect being more pronounced at higher energies and further emphasizing the importance of considering the full band structure. Our study underlines the value of investigating the residual hybridizations and correlation values in the impurity model, with a special emphasis on the $s$-$d$ hybridizations, for a more accurate understanding of the spectral functions. Additionally, we analyzed the implications of these results on the classification of SrMnO$_3$ as an intermediate coupling system. With the $s$-$d$ hybridizations included, we found that the system can be accurately modeled as a weakly coupled system at high temperatures and an intermediate coupled system at lower temperatures, with this classification, however, being based on the $s$-$d$ hybridizations in the impurity model. Our study provides a valuable insight into the physics of transition metal oxides, with a special emphasis on the $s$-$d$ hybridizations, and the results obtained from this study are expected to be relevant to other similar systems.

To facilitate this new framework, we've developed a method to accurately estimate the dimension-five parameter space when starting from the four-dimensional representation, taking into account various combinations of signals and noise. Our analysis suggests that adopting this new framework could lead to a 30% improvement in recovering binary signals that are too faint for current detectors to identify. As future detectors like LIGO Plus and the upgraded LIGO will likely detect binary signals at lower sensitivity levels, employing our new five-dimensional model will be crucial in enhancing their detection sensitivity. As a result, we expect this new framework to become a vital tool in the advanced gravitational wave astronomy era. One key factor hindering the widespread adoption of decentralized energy communities is the high upfront cost of energy storage. A potential solution to overcome this hurdle involves a storage pre-order mechanism that incentivizes participants to invest in storage systems, thus creating a stable demand for encrypted storage and, in turn, fostering trust in decentralized energy trading. However, implementing such a mechanism requires careful consideration of several challenges, including modeling participant planning behavior, managing the storage pre-order process, handling market operations behind a union of paths in a distributed graph, and minimizing pre-order costs while ensuring timely storage commissioning. To address these concerns, a self-planning approach for participants in the storage pre-order process is proposed, utilizing a hybrid method that combines exact and heuristic algorithms, leverages decentralized learning for participant incentive calculation, and employs a generalized version of the flow optimization framework suitable for distributed markets. The proposed self-planning approach is then demonstrated with actual data from the German energy market, yielding promising results for reducing pre-order costs and accelerating storage commissioning. Furthermore, the study explores various policy parameters affecting the self-planning strategy, providing valuable insights for the design of suitable participant incentives. The implemented storage pre-order protocol is freely available for further exploration and adaptation. Through the self-planning approach, a day-ahead market schedule that considers participant storage commissioning, as well as a causal dynamic program for managing real-time storage pre-orders, is produced. This technique allows for extremely accurate testing of quantum mechanics' prediction for electron propagation and can provide insights into complex processes like solid-state phenomena and biochemical reactions. We studied nickel using an x-ray free-electron laser and showed that an extremely short, spatially coherent electron pulse can be produced when an intense x-ray photon beam and an electric field coincide, specifically at the time when the 2p electron wave packet's propagation begins (125 attoseconds). This electron pulse's spatial coherence can be manipulated by changing the initial electron momentum or the time when the x-ray photon beam and the electric field interact. If this electron pulse is directed at a nickel target, then it can produce a spatially coherent photon beam that shows changes in polarization up to 10 attoseconds before the Auger electron arrival time, which can be controlled by changing the initial electron momentum or the time when the x-ray photon beam and the electric field interact. This means that the relative strength of the left and right circularly polarized components of this photon beam can also be controlled over a 20 attosecond period, which is relevant to understanding processes like the optical nuclear polarization effect, and it demonstrates the potential to create a key component called an x-ray vortex beam. Furthermore, this technique allows for the production of a spatially coherent electron-positron pair wave function in as short as 500 attoseconds, which could be useful for accurately studying positronium in flight. This technique's potential to accurately control electron dynamics in matter makes it a valuable tool for better understanding various processes and developing new methods for producing unique particle states. Planetary atmospheres, particularly those of gas giants, exhibit varying rotation periods which affect their circulation patterns. To study this, we developed two simplified global circulation models, one incorporating full planetary rotation and another mimicking the system's natural rotation using a corotating frame. By comparing the results, we found that the latter model accurately represents the former in terms of circulation patterns when the rotation period is short. However, as the rotation period increases, the latter model fails to capture the regime of super-rotation. Additionally, we identified that the model's inability to replicate short-wave turbulence at longer rotation periods results from an incorrect tidal-type forcing, leading to an incorrect phase lag. To rectify this, we modified the model to account for the correct tidal-type forcing, obtaining a more accurate representation of atmospheric circulation patterns. Furthermore, our study provides a framework for understanding atmospheric circulation patterns in planetary systems with stochastic natural rotation. To apply this, we incorporated a measure of atmospheric turbulence into the model, successfully replicating the regime of geostrophic turbulence. Our study provides a foundation for investigating atmospheric circulation patterns in planetary systems with multiple planets, influencing global circulation patterns, to be explored in a forthcoming study. Our models and methods are publicly available and can be adapted to analyze data from spacecraft observations and synthetic systems. The vast majority of learning methods used in Deep Neural Networks are based on optimizing a single objective function that represents the classification accuracy. This standard approach fails to account for the intricate relationships within data that can significantly impact learning, particularly when working with vast datasets like ImageNet. Our research introduces a novel dynamic learning framework that takes into consideration the implicit hierarchies within data, by utilizing a binary tree-like structure to prioritize data points based on their overall magnitude. This approach results in a non-stationary loss function, which the framework effectively addresses through a dynamic adjustment mechanism. Our experiments show that this learning method achieves superior performance when compared to the current state-of-the-art techniques, as seen in the improved results on the ImageNet dataset. Specifically, our model achieves a top-1 accuracy of 9.3%, outperforming other methods, and when using a larger model, it reaches a top-1 accuracy of 12.3%. Our approach is particularly appealing for large-scale learning problems, as it exhibits a significant reduction in the required number of epochs, resulting in substantial decreases in training costs. Our code is openly accessible on the MIMIC repository on GitHub, awaiting further evaluations from the community. With this learning method, we were able to achieve the second-highest accuracy on the ImageNet dataset in the top-1 category in the evaluation benchmarks updated until April 2023. Our research also explores the application of this dynamic learning approach to the selection of neural network models, as well as its potential use in the seamless integration of contrastive learning techniques, although these explorations are considered secondary in this study. Additionally, our results on the CIFAR-100 dataset, along with further analysis on the dynamics of learning at the data point level, are provided in the appendix. This study introduces novel algebraic and geometric aspects of the frequency algebra, a key component of time-frequency analysis. Specifically, it defines the frequency algebra as a $\mathcal{C}^*$-algebra and explores its representation in operator algebra. Moreover, it identifies the frequency algebra with the algebra of absolute moments of a subnormal Toeplitz operator, whose properties mirror those of the classical polynomial algebra. Additionally, it demonstrates that the frequency algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of operators whose absolute moments are finite, with this isomorphism being equivalent to the Schur test for the boundedness of operators. Furthermore, this work establishes an affinity between the frequency algebra and the algebra of operators with the Schur property, both being equivalent to the algebra of operators whose absolute moments are finite. Lastly, it presents an open problem concerning the relationship between the frequency algebra and the algebra of multipliers in Fock spaces. This research is an expansion of earlier work by the first author with P. Rambout, and both versions of the paper are now freely available under the terms of the CC-BY 4.0 license. Moreover, this study has been recognized as a notable contribution and has been included in the journal's 'Best Articles' collection. We have determined that it is possible to control the energy spectrum in these areas by adjusting the width of a trench, which has a significant impact on quantum point contact behavior.  Experimental results demonstrate that it is feasible to observe the on-demand creation of massless Dirac particles near a trench's edges and potentially achieve long-distance quantum transport by adjusting the trench's width.  However, our actual findings show that it is difficult to achieve this criterion with our current sample parameters.  Instead of the expected non-quantized resistance values, we observed resistance values that were close to those predicted for a normal quantum point contact.  The reason for this discrepancy was further investigated and the results obtained are relevant to the study of quantum transport in Dirac materials.  By incorporating a strong in-plane magnetic field, it is possible to switch from the normal Dirac spectrum to the gapless one and vice versa.  This, in turn, allows for the control of backscattering and resulting resistance values, providing a means to achieve targeted resistance quantization.  Notably, when the Dirac spectrum is gapless, resistance values were found to be 12.7 kΩ, in contrast to the expected zero resistance in this configuration.  Furthermore, it was observed that even when the Dirac spectrum is normal, targeted resistance quantization can be achieved with low magnetic field strength.  These discoveries hold the potential to further our understanding of the relationship between magnetic field and quantum transport in HgTe-based systems.  The movement of charge, measured by conductance, can be driven by both a high-frequency potential and a direct electric field applied to a trench. Wireless communication technologies hold tremendous potential to enhance safety and efficiency in urban traffic management, but they face unique challenges due to the unpredictable nature of traffic conditions. In this research, we focus on optimizing communication performance at road intersections using a novel adaptive protocol called NOMA-CAP, which combines Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access with channel adaptation. To evaluate the effectiveness of this protocol, we developed a simulation model that accounts for variables such as traffic light settings, vehicle movement patterns, and interference levels. Our simulations indicate that NOMA-CAP can achieve superior results, outperforming both orthogonal transmission methods and standard NOMA implementations. To further analyze the results, we employed a method called sensitivity analysis, which reveals that the main factors influencing performance are the traffic light cycle length and vehicle speed. However, it is interesting to note that there is no clear correlation between the number of traffic lights and communication performance. Ultimately, our findings provide valuable insights for optimizing urban traffic communication systems, suggesting that careful consideration of traffic light settings may be just as crucial as slowing down interference. In the context of this study, slowing down interference refers to the use of a high gain directional antenna at the base station, which significantly improves performance. As a result, vehicles with high speed profiles experience better performance with shorter traffic light cycles, while those with low speed profiles perform better with longer cycles. Furthermore, there is an interesting phenomenon where increasing the traffic light cycle beyond a certain point may actually lead to decreased performance due to increased exposure to interference. In terms of future development, our research indicates that the next generation of urban traffic communication systems should prioritize the use of high gain directional antennas, large code blocks, and adaptive transmission protocols to achieve even better results. Ultimately, it is essential to strike a balance between system performance and the practical considerations of implementing new technologies in real-world settings. As a result, there is a great potential for further research in this area, specifically in the evaluation of future traffic light control strategies using advanced communication systems, as well as the development of more efficient and adaptable communication protocols tailored to the unique characteristics of urban traffic scenarios. In the long-term, this could enable the creation of a new class of large-scale urban scenarios that could be used to validate the performance of next-generation communication systems, leading to even more innovative and efficient traffic management solutions. Additionally, this kind of research could pave the way for the development of new peer-to-peer communication protocols, such as NOMA-CAP, that could be adapted to various types of interference and may be suitable for integration with traditional cellular systems

This square has an interesting property where two of its corners, denoted as A and C, have cardinals that are finite with respect to the global algebra, whereas the other two corners, B and D, have an infinite cardinal with respect to the global algebra. This construction builds upon previous work by the author with Terry Shorr, where a 16^2 square with a similar structure was created but with the difference that one of its corners had a finite cardinal that was infinite with respect to the global algebra. This new development has implications for the index of subfactors and set theoretical free groups. Recent research on Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) exhibits remarkable performance in trading optimization and portfolio management tasks. Notably, HNNs can achieve results on par with those of Linear Genetic Algorithms (LGAs), despite being trained via backpropagation on a hamiltonian mechanics-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) approximation. This study aims to investigate whether HNNs can acquire useful gradients by exploring the properties of the Hamiltonian Neural Network objective function. To this end, we employ both qualitative and quantitative analysis methods to examine the outcomes of training HNNs with various optimization techniques. Our results show that certain optimization strategies result in negligible gradient norms, which we characterize as the 'gradient-free' scenario. In contrast, other optimization methods yield non-negligible gradient norms, which we term the 'gradient-dominated' scenario. Ultimately, our research reveals that the former scenario yields superior performance in benchmark tasks. Given the numerous applications of HNNs in optimization and control contexts, our findings carry significant implications, and we anticipate our contributions to inspire further research into the behavior of HNNs. In complex systems with multiple agents, ensuring the highest level of performance across all actions is crucial. To achieve this, it's essential to maintain the reliability of the agents' decision-making process. When machine learning models are trained to make decisions, it's common for them to operate in a environment where they can influence how the data is updated, effectively becoming part of an adversarial feedback loop. This phenomenon can lead to decreased performance over time, particularly when the models are vulnerable to sudden changes or rare events. This work introduces an innovative multi-agent approach, where a human is an active participant in the process, providing trust ratings for the predictions made by the models. This trust information is used to adjust the loss function to focus on the predictions the human considers reliable. As the system learns, it identifies patterns that may indicate areas where the models' performance is inconsistent or unstable. To address this, the system proactively seeks more data from the human to refine its understanding of the situation. This way, the performance of the models is continuously optimized based on the human's trust ratings. This approach is a human-in-the-loop, online multi-agent method that achieves consistent high levels of performance, compared to traditional reinforcement learning methods, according to our experiments. This approach is applicable across various domains, as demonstrated by our experiments on both classification and regression problems, and even shows positive results in a real-world application. Detecting prohibited items, such as explosives, narcotics, and weapons, is crucial for maintaining public safety at airports and other high-risk locations. Although X-ray technology is commonly used for this purpose, some of its limitations hinder its effectiveness, especially when it comes to low-contrast objects. To enhance the performance of X-ray security screening, researchers have been exploring various post-processing techniques in recent years. Despite the release of the OpenSet dataset, a widely used benchmark for evaluating the security screening process, there are still significant challenges to be addressed, primarily stemming from its restricted size and unsuitable annotation, which significantly impede the development of practical solutions. To address this issue, a new superior benchmark called Advanced OpenSet has been created, comprising a substantially larger and more diverse dataset with annotated background regions that serve as reference points for prohibited items. To further improve the performance of prohibited item detection, a novel module called Lateral Suppression Module has been designed, capable of identifying items located near the image boundary. When tested on the newly created Advanced OpenSet dataset, as well as the OpenSet dataset, LSM module demonstrates its effectiveness, outperforming existing detection methods, such as DeepSort and DFNet. The advanced dataset and proposed module, consisting of a lateral suppression module using Convolutional Neural Networks, can be accessed through a publicly available repository. According to evaluation results, the proposed method obtains impressive performance on both the OpenSet and Advanced OpenSet datasets, achieving mean average precision (AP) scores of 0.897 and 0.914, respectively. To facilitate real-world implementation, the proposed system is designed for real-time operation, capable of processing 30 frames per second on a desktop computer. Furthermore, the scalability of the dataset and the simplicity of the proposed module's architecture make it suitable for integration with other systems, while the repository containing the dataset's annotation and the module's code can be easily shared with other researchers. The creation of the Advanced OpenSet dataset, along with the Lateral Suppression Module, provides an enhanced framework for developing practical prohibited item detection solutions. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, exhaustive experiments comparing its performance to state-of-the-art techniques have been conducted, confirming the superiority of the new dataset and detection module. The terminology used for describing prohibited items, such as narcotics, explosives, and weapons, has been standardized in line with international norms, while the development of the Advanced OpenSet dataset has addressed the limitations of existing datasets by increasing diversity, while the Lateral Suppression Module outperformed competing detection methods

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in WSD, albeit the improvements are often confined to the development dataset and tend to stagnate on unseen data.  One key reason for this challenge is the quality of training data, which is notable for containing incomplete or misleading context information.  In response to this issue, we propose a novel approach called Context-gloss Augmentation, which involves using a pre-existing base of semantic relations to generate context sentences that are both relevant and accurate for the words in question.  By integrating this method into the BERT-based WSD framework, we are able to enhance the learning process with reliable context information, even in cases where the words are presented alone.  Our results indicate that this approach yields a notable boost in WSD performance, as evidenced by the improved overall accuracy achieved with a unified model across five distinct datasets.  The code for our context-gloss augmentation method has been made publicly available on GitHub.  Furthermore, we have established a new benchmark called Context-gloss Relatedness Dataset, which involves testing the ability of models to recognize context sentences that are relevant or misleading to a particular word with a specific sense.  This benchmark holds the potential to direct future research towards enhancing the context quality of training datasets, which is critical for improving the performance of WSD systems in real-world applications.  We have also explored an alternative application of our Context-gloss Augmentation method, referred to as Context-gloss Refinement, which involves fine-tuning a pre-trained model to recognize high-quality context information even after the addition of noisy data.  We have validated our approach through multiple experiments and have achieved promising results, which indicate that a part of the semantic relation data with low quality can be distinguished from high-quality data, and that a model trained on our Context-gloss Augmentation method is capable of prioritizing reliable context information over less reliable alternatives.  We have provided quantitative and qualitative analysis of our results, which provide insight into the relationship between context quality and WSD performance.  We have identified several potential directions for future research, which could direct the attention of the research community towards the study of context and related topics, such as Context Decoding and Context Augmentation, which are both crucial for improving the performance of WSD systems in real-world applications. This analysis formulates the extended Gamma function using an integral expression that has been optimized for a regularized integral transformation. The optimized formulation employs a critical cutoff threshold to define the function's domain, resulting in a modified integral expression that incorporates a Gaussian integral and arises from the integration of the reciprocal Gamma function over a finite period. The study investigates various regularized forms of this modified integral expression, including both a direct cutoff method and a more complex indirect approach. The latter involves the use of a logarithmic function and yields a particularly intriguing result, revealing that the standard Gamma function can be expressed as a combination of two of these regularized integral expressions. The research also demonstrates that both regularized forms lead to the derivation of the Gamma function's minimory property, while the indirect approach provides a novel proof of the function's recurrence relationship. The study concludes by exploring a potential connection to the concept of volume, suggesting that the reciprocal Gamma function may be an integral part of a more comprehensive framework that encompasses both the Gamma function and the Riemann zeta function. The analysis emphasizes the significance of selecting a suitable regularized form to prevent the emergence of divergent paths, paving the way for further investigations into the properties and applications of the extended Gamma function. The study's results may offer valuable insights for fields such as mathematical physics and number theory, while the development of a more rigorous justification for the chosen regularized form remains an exciting direction for future research. An analysis of proton-nucleus data by the LHCb experiment suggests testing the top quark's generation hypothesis, which could potentially validate the extension of the Standard Model known as the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. This approach creates challenging situations for systems to be tested and evaluated by automatically producing difficult road networks in the form of Bezier curves. By focusing on a specific type of curve known as second-degree simple loops, a mathematical framework is established to analyze its properties. However, this approach falls short as it cannot efficiently represent many modern road networks, which are made up of loops of higher degrees. To address this limitation, a more comprehensive framework incorporating higher-degree loops is introduced. Nevertheless, this more comprehensive framework is not without its drawbacks, as it introduces issues related to navigation, reduces the system's overall efficiency, and incorporates unnecessary complex curves, which deviate from the typical characteristics of most road networks. In an effort to restore the practicality of this method, a more limited version of the loop structure is reconsidered, which results in a combination of both high and low degree loops. A new class of hydrodynamic equations is proposed to accurately model interacting Bose gases in various random phase-space environments.  The proposed equations are consistently derived from first principles using a quantum hydrodynamic approach that takes into account the interconnections between quantum, thermal, and random phase-space motion.  The new equations are then applied to the specific case of a zero-mean random phase-space environment, resulting in modified Klein-Gordon equations that account for the effects of this randomness.  The predictions of the model are validated by comparing its results to existing studies of a one-dimensional, repulsive Bose gas in a random potential.  The equations also reveal a random potential-induced shift in the barometric scale and a enhancement of the speed of sound, both of which can be measured using a displaced Gaussian trial wave function.  Furthermore, the proposed equations are shown to be applicable to quantum gases confined to harmonic oscillator and Coulomb potentials.  The model is particularly useful for describing the dynamics of Bose-Einstein condensates in mouth organs, human vocal cords, and other musical instrument sources, such as violins and cellos.  The equations are set to be tested experimentally using high-resolution velocity-sound wave interferometry.  The model can be extended to also describe non-interacting Fermi gases as well as interacting Fermi and Bose gases.  The BEC-NEF phase boundary obtained from the model agrees with existing numerical simulations for the study of interacting Bose-Einstein condensates.  The model is a crucial breakthrough for the development of an efficient quantum computer algorithm, based on an analytical transformation of the Hamiltonian, that can efficiently simulate the dynamics of interacting Bose gases in random phase-space environments.  The proposed equations provide a new fundamental understanding of quantum gases in random phase-space environments, describing the unique phenomena these systems exhibit, such as the non-monetary BEC-NEF phase boundary, and the non-monetary increase of the speed of sound in these systems.  The model is a significant advancement in the field of quantum hydrodynamics, and it is expected to have a major impact on the experimental and theoretical study of interacting Bose gases in random phase-space environments, leading to the development of new quantum computer algorithms and potentially discovering new phenomena in this field.  The proposed equations, in conjunction with velocity-sound wave interferometry, will allow for the precise measurement of the speed of sound in these systems, providing a clear path for experimental verification of the model's predictions and further validation of its applications. However, the field lacks a standard benchmark that comprehensively assesses the capabilities of pre-trained models in such environments. To address this gap, we introduce a new ongoing learning benchmark, based on a dynamic platform that allows us to systematically examine the challenges posed by continuously arriving data. This benchmark enables us to evaluate the implications of four crucial factors that characterize ongoing learning, using a unified framework that can be applied to multiple target tasks. Utilizing a suite of pre-trained models, we investigate how they perform on our benchmark, and our results reveal that while these models excel in static settings, they can struggle with ongoing learning, with some even experiencing deterioration in performance. However, selecting the optimal model parameters often involves a trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. Another common issue with machine learning experiments is the challenge of evaluating models with limited training data. Cross-validation is a widely accepted method to mitigate these problems, by assessing model performance based on multiple subsets of the data rather than a single split. Despite its widespread adoption, the standard k-fold CV approach can result in biased parameter settings that may not accurately represent the model's performance. This tendency becomes more pronounced in Natural Language Processing, where models are inherently prone to overfitting. Our results indicate that J-K fold CV yields superior performance compared to standard k-fold CV and grid search, significantly outperforming it on multiple NLP tasks. We find that using small sub-groups (K=5) and a larger number of sub-groups (J=3) results in the best performance, reducing the risk of overfitting associated with standard k-fold CV. We believe our research will guide other NLP researchers to select the most effective hyperparameter settings for their models, potentially leading to better performance in NLP tasks. We decide to share our findings with the broader machine learning community, with the hope that J-K fold CV will become a widely accepted method for model evaluation, with possible applications in other domain science tasks. Intelligent agents in various settings, including education, benefit greatly from pre-trained knowledge bases, which do not natively incorporate pupil data. The need for a knowledge acquisition process that can effectively train these models using an instructor has given rise to a specific type of machine learning framework, which has become known as the Instructor-Pupil (InP) framework. This survey provides a comprehensive examination of the InP framework, along with its adaptations in contexts beyond education, where it shares many practical applications. We proceed with a detailed exploration of existing InP variants, before exploring potential extensions to the basic InP model and addressing key challenges associated with the InP paradigm. Ultimately, we outline promising research directions for the InP framework as a whole.

We address this challenge by testing the assumption that a static optimal solution exists and can be identified through full system knowledge. Instead, we find that the best approach is a dynamic, adaptive method that leverages online learning and robust optimization. By assuming components' cost functions can be measured precisely and there is sufficient time to adjust to changing costs, we prove that an adaptive policy achieves a similar performance to the optimal static solution. When these conditions are not met, we propose a revised framework that accommodates partial system knowledge and delayed adaptation, resulting in a suboptimal but stable solution. Our results demonstrate the method's effectiveness through numerical examples and real-world applications. Furthermore, we explore ways to reduce the computational expense of this approach. One potential improvement involves examining a more complex adaptive strategy that can result in a more efficient solution but requires additional assumptions about robust convergence. Our research examines the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry is removed, we observe an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Notably, we observed that $v_3$ polarisation towards the second and third quadrants is negative, indicating a notable tripartite relationship with multiparticle correlations. Finally, we extracted centrality-dependent radial flow contributions from combined $v_2$ and $v_3$ data using a hydrodynamic model, verifying our transport model's results. These findings reinforce the tripartite nature of flow phenomena, Rooted in initial geometric conditions. Furthermore, they emphasize the intricate relationship between elliptical and triangular flow. In essence, our analysis presents a unified description of flow phenomena through their geometric origins, uncovering an intricate tripartite structure. Ultimately, this understanding shall serve as a pivotal landmark in the pursuit of flow's underlying principles. In the context of our research, we propose a landmark that symbolises this discovery, integrating elements from geometry and flow. Specifically, we introduce the $\Delta$ quantity, defined as the difference between a particle's flow amplitude and the flow amplitude of the same type but with an opposite alignment. In our research, we have the case of $v_2$ and $v_3$, but conceptually, $\Delta$ can be applied to any flow type. This new metric provides a clear and direct measurement of flow's polarisation, making it an essential tool for the interpretation of experimental data. This problem is further complicated by limited, difficult-to-access, and sometimes secure edge devices. To overcome these difficulties, we propose a new testing approach, called Event-Focused Testing, that allows for the simulation of edge environments using any available device. By leveraging virtualization and network simulation tools, this method creates a degree of abstraction between the application under test and the edge infrastructure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Event-Focused Testing by developing a test framework for an open-source edge platform, and the results show that it can efficiently handle a variety of edge use cases, including those that require low latency and real-time data transmission. Furthermore, this method enables the simulation of different edge setups, such as varying numbers of devices and different network conditions, without the need for explicit driver support. We also explore ways to integrate Event-Focused Testing with existing testing frameworks and discuss the potential for this method to be applied to other types of distributed systems. The LHC has yielded a substantial amount of data at an energy level where tree-level processes that break CP symmetry are prominent. As a result, several experiments have increased their sensitivity to measuring CP-violating phenomena in various processes. This poster is an overview of the latest findings from the ATLAS collaboration regarding CP violation and rare decays involving beauty mesons. It covers recent results concerning the CP asymmetry in charm and bottom hadron production, as well as results for the rare decays $B^0_s \to \phi \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $B^0 \to K^0 \pi^0$. It also includes results for the searches $B^0 \to K^0 K^0$ and $B^0 \to K^0 \pi^0 \pi^0$. Furthermore, it highlights the current sensitivity of the ATLAS experiment to the lepton flavor universality violating process $B^0 \to K^0 \ell^+ \ell^-$. It is essential to note that the abundance of data as well as the precision of the measurements have not been reflected in the current limits presented in this report. Consequently, many of the existing bounds have been re-evaluated in light of new data, and a significant portion of the existing literature can be surpassed by the updated limits. In contrast, several existing limits remain highly competitive with the current findings from the BEAUTY and LHCb collaborations. It is worth noting that the ATLAS experiment can anticipate a substantial enhancement in sensitivity to these processes upon completion of the Level-1 muon trigger system upgrade. In addition, it is expected that the upgraded LHC with an increased luminosity and higher collision energy will provide the BEAUTY and LHCb collaborations with significantly more sensitive results in the future. In this poster, the current findings from the ATLAS collaboration, combined with the anticipated breakthroughs that will arise from upgrades to the detector and the upgraded LHC, are presented. For autonomous navigation, Scene Flow Estimation (SFE) plays a critical role as it generates both optical flow and depth information. While many SFE methods excel in controlled environments, they struggle with real-world applications. A significant challenge in achieving this is by leveraging information from surrounding pixels with varying importance, which can lead to inconsistent training signals. To address this issue, a common technique used is to minimize the mean squared error between predicted flow and reference data. However, this approach has several drawbacks: it prioritizes the average case, neglects outliers, and doesn't consider the metric properties of flow data. To overcome these limitations, a new objective function based on the Mahalanobis distance is proposed, which is more robust and takes into account the specific pixel correlations. To further improve, a new model was developed, which combines a bi-directional encoder decoder network for better initializations and more accurate estimations. The proposed method was extensively tested and compared with state-of-the-art methods on datasets used for training and never seen before tests, proving its effectiveness. In recent years, Random Neural Networks (RNNs) have gained interest due to their versatility in tackling classification tasks, particularly those involving the recognition of images, speech, and handwritten text. Despite the benefits of RNNs, current implementations of them, particularly those based on spike-tracing methods, can be computationally costly and energy-hungry when used for categorization purposes. To address this issue, we propose a novel, reduced-complexity RNN model that utilizes spike-tracing for categorization, where neurons are assigned to specific classes based on unique layer configurations. This model minimizes unnecessary spike communications and silent spikes during training, achieving lower latency, energy consumption, and overall computation costs compared to traditional RNNs. To validate our approach, we conducted numerous training and testing experiments with various datasets, including the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ResISC45, and our results show that our revised RNN model matches the accuracy of traditional RNNs while significantly reducing latency, energy consumption, and computation costs. Furthermore, our model requires minimal training time and outperforms current spike-tracing methods based on gradient descent. To facilitate the integration of our model into neuromorphic hardware platforms, we developed a novel spike-coded categorization method that replaces the activation function with a linear function, enabling easy classification of inputs. Overall, our revised RNN model provides a precise and energy-efficient solution for categorization tasks on neuromorphic hardware. To showcase the practical application of our model, we designed a real-world application, namely a driver-assistance system, utilizing the ResISC45 dataset, and successfully implemented it using the TrueNorth neuromorphic chip. Our code is available online for the reproducibility of our results. To further improve the performance of our model, we explored the integration of a linear layer and a small number of additional neurons, which resulted in an even higher classification accuracy and lower computation costs. Our study indicates that the optimal parameters of our model depend on the type of dataset being used, and future work should focus on the relaxation of the requirement for precise spike timing. To facilitate the seamless transition between spiking and non-spiking neural networks, we propose the integration of a spike-to-burst converter, which enables easy transition between the two approaches.
