A new classification for cubic graphs is introduced based on ideal pairings, a concept inspired by the Hamiltonian property. The relationship between this classification and two other properties - the existence of a Hamiltonian circuit and the ability to tint the edges with a specific set - is examined. A connection is established between the proposed classification and these properties, with implications for the Grotzch theorem. Additionally, this is explored in the context of a subcategory of cubic graphs, defined by the requirement that all 3-cycles in these graphs are Hamiltonian. This is represented mathematically using a set of constraints based on the Jones polynomials. A more practical application of this is the identification of a specific class of cubic graphs, defined by the presence of particular Hamiltonian triplets and an edge that can be tinted. This is further analyzed in terms of its ideal pairings and Hamiltonian triplets. A notable feature of this is the presence of a Hamiltonian circuit, as well as the ability to tint all edges with a set that meets a specific condition - being orthogonal to the set defined by the graph's structure. This is then used to derive a new graph, constructed through a process called edge-union. This new graph is shown to have a Hamiltonian circuit and the ability to tint all its edges with a set that meets a certain condition. Furthermore, this property is inherited by a sub-class of graphs derived from it, although interestingly this does not extend to all graphs in this family - indicating a need for further differentiation within this category. A specific graph within this class, derived from the Clebsch graph, is shown to have a Hamiltonian circuit and the ability to tint all its edges with a set that meets a certain condition. This is then used to demonstrate the application of this theory to a higher-degree graphs - utilizing the edge-union construction to derive new 6-degree graphs from the cubic graphs. A new challenge is also presented - identifying all the cubic graphs that can be tinted with a set that meets a specific condition - and proving that one of the derived 6-degree graphs, constructed through edge-union from the Clebsch graph, can be tinted with a set that meets a certain condition, although it does not have a Hamiltonian circuit. This is further analyzed in terms of its ideal pairings and Hamiltonian triplets. A new method called edge-tinting is proposed, along with a new formula for calculating the number of edges that can be tinted with a set that meets a specific condition

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. Furthermore, we establish the conditions under which we can achieve spectral or orbital stability within a specific gauge. Specifically, we establish the requirement for the anharmonic oscillator's potential to exhibit a double-well structure and certain properties of the Klein-Gordon equation's potential in order to guarantee the spectral stability of the solitary wave state. We establish the condition for orbital stability as the solitary wave state being a critical point within the symmetric space defined by the Hamiltonian associated with the linearized equation. We apply and verify our theory by specifically analyzing a Klein-Gordon equation joined to a perturbed Kalabugh-Bessler-Scott anharmonic oscillator and a Klein-Gordon equation joined to a perturbed Rosenau-Hiebert anharmonic oscillator. Both of these anharmonic oscillators fail to meet the required stability criteria. Conversely, we demonstrate that both of these anharmonic oscillators' equations do achieve orbital stability for solitary waves under a different, non-symmetric gauge. This particular result holds the potential for further simplification. We also introduce a more manageable, though still abstract, concept of 2π-periodic orbital stability to encompass cases where the anharmonic oscillator's potential exhibits a n-fold (n>=3) winded structure. This new definition holds the potential for further exploration and development. Ultimately, this study is an expansion of prior works by Berti-Luke and Holmer-Schmitt on the Klein-Gordon equation joined to an harmonic oscillator, both of which are incorporated as a specific case. This study provides a more general framework that surpasses the scope of those works. It is also a continuation of the author's earlier study on the Dirac equation joined to an anharmonic oscillator, which is incorporated as a front-line case. The concept of cooperation is fundamental to both individual success and the progress of society as a whole. Understanding cooperation within academic networks can provide valuable insights to promote collaborative work and the dissemination of knowledge. However, the complexity of these dynamics makes them challenging to study. This paper delves into the analysis of academic cooperation using an extensive dataset from the DBLP database, with a focus on dynamic aspects and weak ties. By incorporating temporal features into their network measurements and identifying the specific characteristics of central actors, researchers were able to observe the evolution of cooperation and the formation of new relationships. Their findings reveal key patterns in the development of scholarly cooperation and the importance of weak ties in driving innovation and the search for new knowledge. Additionally, they propose a novel method for measuring centrality that takes into account both an actor's immediate connections and their broader position within the network. This approach can be applied to a wide range of temporal and weighted network datasets. Furthermore, they demonstrate the efficacy of their proposed centrality measure, drawing from a literary co-authorship network and a network of scholars who have attended and presented at prestigious conferences. This work can contribute to the development of more effective strategies for promoting cooperation and the transmission of knowledge within academic networks. By applying their analysis to other types of complex networks characterized by dynamic relationships, their findings can further reveal crucial insights into the principles of cooperation that underlie such networks. This work has been designed to be of interest to multiple fields, including the study of social networks, the spread of ideas, literary co-authorships, and academic collaborations. It is hoped that this research will also be useful to practitioners working in collaboration technology and social network analysis. This paper details a specialized device used to study the production of spallation neutrons in Aberdeen's underground research facility. The Aberdeen Tunnel facility, with its 80-meter layer of rock above it, provides an ideal setting to investigate spallation neutron production caused by high-energy muons. Due to the difficulty of directly measuring these particles, researchers have developed a large-scale detector system consisting of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors. Each layer contains 32 individual detectors, extending 20 meters into the tunnel, and is designed to identify the direction and energy of the incoming muons. Between the plastic-scintillator layers, there are five layers of helium-filled gas detectors, serving as a secondary neutron detector system. This combined system allows for the simultaneous measurement of neutron production across the entire tunnel, significantly increasing its statistical accuracy. Furthermore, it can distinguish between the contributions of incoming muons and secondary muons generated by the interaction of incoming neutrons with the rock. This device will greatly contribute to the assessment of large-scale rock neutron production facilities, such as future long-term neutron sources like the Aberdeen-based PRISM facility. Due to its versatility, it can also be adapted to measure neutron production caused by high-energy protons or heavy ions. The TESS-Keck Survey aims to investigate how planetary systems interact with their host stars through a large-scale study of tidal disruption events (TDEs). To achieve this, researchers selected 8000 candidates targets using the TESS Galactic distribution. From this pool, they identified 541 TDEs based on brightness variations. To validate these findings, a spectroscopic analysis was conducted using Keck II, ultimately resulting in 137 TDEs with confirmed host star properties. By linking TDEs to their stars, scientists were able to establish a relationship between black hole mass and star type, and also establish that a significant portion of TDEs (approximately 17%) occur in low-mass star systems not accounted for in prior studies. Additionally, a comparison with stellar populations near the Milky Way's plane revealed an underrepresented population of TDEs, and a striking difference in intermediate-mass star TDE rates (which were found to be 8.5±1.5×10^-3 yr^-1) when comparing the survey area to areas outside the plane. Furthermore, when controlling for detection biases, a rate of 5.8±1.3×10^-3 yr^-1 was found for the entire TESS-Keck Survey area, providing a rate that is consistent with prior studies. However, little research has been conducted to evaluate the impact of differential privacy on the performance of deep neural networks. Furthermore, there is no clear understanding of how hyperparameters influence the trade-off between security and accuracy. In this paper, we investigate the effect of various hyperparameters on the balance between security and accuracy in deep neural networks. Our analysis reveals that introducing noise in the forward path has a negative impact on the network's accuracy, whereas masking input data has a limited impact. The success of deep learning in various tasks depends on its ability to minimize a specific loss function, which is often chosen based on problem assumptions and empirical observations. Despite its importance, the loss function is frequently considered a fixed component in deep learning networks, subject to adjustment without scrutiny. This study challenges this assumption by examining a fundamental question: What impact does the selection of loss function have on the performance of a neural network, assuming all other factors remain constant? To this end, our research evaluates the influence of loss function alterations by comparing the performance of multiple loss function variants of a fixed network architecture, trained under identical conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that even minor adjustments to the loss function can lead to substantial performance differences, resulting in potential improvements or degradation of up to 10%. Furthermore, our analysis identifies key factors that contribute to these variations, including network regularization, convergence rates, and label distribution, providing insights that can inform the design of future neural networks. To facilitate further exploration, our study introduces a metrics-driven framework for evaluating loss function variants, which is adaptable to different classification scenarios. In conclusion, our research underscores the significance of careful loss function selection and systematic evaluation in deep learning, emphasizing the need to view the loss function as a core component of the network, subject to continuous optimization and refinement. By extending this perspective, we may derive more innovative loss function designs that extract deeper insights from annotated data, ultimately propelling the field of deep learning forward. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with a boundary feedback operator that maintains the skew-symmetry of the control. The constructed controller achieves global asymptotic stability for the closed-loop system, with a Lyapunov function derived from the energy function of the original system. The designed controller can also be represented in a decentralized form, effectively making it a local stability controller. Numerical examples are provided to illustrate the efficacy of the constructed controller. The study extends previous work on the control of viscous fluids by incorporating a boundary feedback operator and demonstrating the asympototic stability of the closed-loop system. The competition between s-wave and d-wave pairings due to magnetic impurities is investigated using the coherent density-necessity approach, considering both paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic scenarios. Our findings show that when the exchange interaction between the triplicate couples and the magnetic impurities is strong, the tripicate couples' region is divided into two sub-regions: one where d-wave pairing dominates over s-wave pairing, and another where s-wave pairing becomes more favored due to the exchange interaction's sign change with the inclusion of magnetic impurities. The result that magnetic impurities can induce a Pauli paramagnetic response in the d-wave paired phase provides a basis for understanding the magnetic impurities' effect on UNClO$_3$. Continuous phase modulation detection using non-coherent differential detection techniques has historically relied on the optimal differential phase shift (ODPS) detector, which serves as its detection method. However, we have discovered that modifying the CPM signal via time-reversal (TR) and phase-shift (PS) transformations results in an increased maximum correlation peak, leading to lower false alarm rates and improved detection performance compared to the standard ODPS detector. Notably, this performance gain can be achieved without compromising the system's noise resistance. Furthermore, our analysis facilitates the derivation of simplified TR-PS differential phase shift (STRPSD) detector bounds, which can result in reduced computational costs. As a demonstration, we analyze the 2PSK CPM scenario under both ideal and phase noise conditions, verifying the delays introduced by the TR-PS transformer and the STRPSD detector. Our results indicate that the TR-PS transformer can result in a 50% decrease in false alarm rates, while the STRPSD detector can achieve comparable performance to the ODPS detector with a 125% increase in detection delay. As such, the TR-PS transformer can be an attractive alternative to the ODPS detector, especially for systems requiring extended detection delays. Our analysis also enables the derivation of TR-PS transformer delays for any CPM scenario, providing a valuable resource for CPM system designers. Our study's results are valuable for CPM system designers, as they can utilize the derived STRPSD bounds or even the delays provided in this study to enhance their system's performance. HD 80606 b is an exoplanet orbiting its host star in an extremely eccentric path. It offers scientists a chance to observe the massive planet interact with its star during its closest point, known as superior conjunction. Researchers have a global network of telescopes observe this planet during this stage of its orbit. By analyzing their data, a revised prediction for when the planet will be at its closest point to its star can be determined, which is crucial for scheduling the Jame Webb Space Telescope's observations. 

In our study, we combine data from multiple telescopes, including the OSIRIS on Haleakala, to calculate the orbital path for the planet. Initially, the team had issues with the planet's interaction with its star due to its fast orbital period. Then, they discovered the problem lay with the initial data being considered, specifically the orbital period being overestimated. By using a more accurate starting point, they were able to calculate the planet's orbital path more precisely. 

Now, they are able to predict the planet's closest point to its star will reoccur on 28th February 2024. This study shows how combining data from multiple telescopes can provide a clearer picture of a planet's orbital path, which is crucial for scheduling the James Webb Space Telescope's observations. 

By considering all available data, researchers can establish a more accurate understanding of a planet's eccentric orbit. This is significant because it can make the most out of the observations provided by state-of-the-art space technology. 

It's also interesting to note that the model developed in this study, in its current form, doesn't take planetary alignment into account. However, the team is open to modifying their model to incorporate this factor if it becomes necessary. 

Lastly, this study provides valuable insights on how to use a worldwide network of telescopes to solve a complex problem, which could be applied to addressing other difficulties that arise during the analysis of astronomical data. 

The data used in this study is publicly accessible and can be utilized by any researcher. The model developed, on the other hand, is proprietary but the team is willing to share the code with any interested scientist. 

In conclusion, this study shows how combining data from multiple telescopes can provide a clearer picture of a planet's orbital path, which is crucial for scheduling the James Webb Space Telescope's observations. This model can be applied to any high-eccentricity planet, which will become more prevalent as more exoplanets are discovered with the launch of the Transiting Exoplan Survey Satellite.

Deep learning models, particularly those utilizing dual-modal training with computed tomography (CT), have demonstrated the potential to enhance PET images by recovering lost information, but they have several limitations: 1) they often prioritize preserving dose levels rather than reducing it, 2) they struggle with accommodating variations in anatomy that go beyond the training dataset, 3) they tend to prioritize structural accuracy over quantitative accuracy, and 4) they typically don't take into account the unique physical properties of PET, such as blurred images resulting from the detection process. This research aims to address these challenges by developing a new deep learning framework that utilizes physical properties of PET imaging to enhance images, while also considering variations in anatomy and unique PET properties. This novel approach, pre-trained with uncertainty-conscious data and incorporating a residual learning strategy to handle out-of-distribution data, resulted in significantly improved PET images at reduced doses, outperforming current state-of-the-art models. Specifically, when using one-fifth of the standard 18FB-floxuridine dose, the proposed method yielded images with good correlation (R2=0.945) to ground truth images obtained at full doses, in contrast to only fair correlation (R2= 0.851) for the best current benchmark. This research was executed with the help of CT and PET scans provided by two major hospitals. The developed model exhibited efficient performance on unseen datasets, demonstrating its potential as a reliable solution for reducing PET doses. The implemented coding technique also ensured reproducibility, as the model was trained and tested using publicly available codes, with the exception of the novel uncertainty-conscious pre-training scheme. The team is now planning to explore additional applications for reduced-dose PET imaging, such as utilizing transformed CT images and incorporating additional multimodal data, as well as exploring new data-driven strategies for determining optimal reduced doses. The implemented model, although initially designed for 18FB-floxuridine, can potentially be adapted for other PET radiotracers with proper retraining, as the unique detection process of PET imaging provides a common basis for all such tracers. This process is heavily influenced by the generation of real and virtual photons that interact with the proton's charge, as well as the formation of $q\bar{q}$ pairs through gluon splitting. The stability of this oscillation is influenced by the filling configuration of the linac, the characteristics of the $q\bar{q}$ pair, and the particle's charge, which determines the particle's reaction to the oscillation's perturbation. The interplay of these factors leads to distinct behaviors of the instability in different cases. For instance, in the case of real photons, the threshold for instability is significantly affected by the linac's wavelength, while in the case of virtual photons, the linac's wavelength has a relatively minor impact. Furthermore, in the case of gluons, the linac's wavelength's impact is similar to that of real photons, which indicates that the nature of the particle has a significant effect on the instability's behavior. Our R library, lfda, allows users to execute LFDA and then visualize its results using dimensionality reduction techniques such as t-SNE, PCA, and UMAP. Additionally, lfda provides a user-friendly interface for clustering analysis and includes the capability to handle missing data through the K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) imputation method. By incorporating internal and external evaluation metrics, lfda offers assessment tools for the quality of its dimensionality reduction outcomes. Moreover, lfda enables the identification of discriminative dimensions or clusters and offers a user-friendly clustering function based on LFDA, along with the option to handle multi-class classification problems. Furthermore, the lfda library includes a personalized dimensionality reduction function, where the dimensionality reduction results can be utilized for the visualization of data points based on their labels. This library aims to facilitate the implementation of LFDA and provide a comprehensive framework for the exploration and visualization of LFDA outcomes. The serial dictatorship method, a widely accepted procedure for allocating a single item among a set of potential buyers in an appropriate order, is a key topic of discussion. We compare the ability of various methods to generate socially desirable outcomes when buyers' valuations are determined by their position in the order in which they place bids. We find that no method can guarantee better results than the standard serial dictatorship approach when buyers' values are independent of their order of placement. However, if values do depend on order, there are scenarios in which the standard approach fails while a new procedure we propose succeeds in achieving a better outcome. We also explore under what conditions a proposed rule is preferred over the standard approach. Additionally, we examine how assigning part of the property's value to one of its attributes can lead to desirable outcomes when values are interdependent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using numerical examples and publicly available data from the National Association of Realtors. Our analysis provides a general framework for evaluating the performance of social choice procedures, extending beyond the specific context of serial dictatorships and revealing potential avenues for further research. We anticipate that our work will contribute usefully to ongoing research into the serial dictatorship method and will offer policymakers a valuable tool for designing allocation processes that prioritize fairness and efficiency. This research focuses on identifying complete, fair, and community sum distinguishing total colorings for various types of circulant graphs. Multi-label learning problems are identified as challenging when the training dataset doesn't provide instance-level labels but instead utilizes class-level labels for all instances sharing the same label. This issue is addressed by a previously developed method called Multi-Label Instance Extraction, which aims to learn multiple labels for a single instance using just a single positive label. A key problem with existing MLE approaches is that they rely on noisy or third-party information to acquire additional labels, which isn't always feasible in practice. A novel multi-label learning framework called Direct MLE is introduced, which enables the extraction of multiple labels from a single positive label without utilizing additional information, thereby making it suitable for real-world applications. A primary contribution of this work is a new Direct MLE model and a comprehensive set of experiments designed to evaluate its performance on various datasets and scenarios. Results indicate that Direct MLE consistently outperforms existing multi-label learning methods using a partially labeled training set, confirming its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on machine learning algorithms to analyze this data, making predictions and providing personalization. However, these models require significant data, are prone to overfitting, and can perpetuate biases - especially when deployed on a diet of binary datasets. This paper presents FedHealth, a pioneering attempt to combine federated learning with transfer learning, capable of handling real-world datasets from wearable devices. FedHealth enables the training of lightweight models using a dataset from one source, and then applies this knowledge to analyze data from a different target dataset, without transferring sensitive user data. We evaluate FedHealth through a series of experiments using the MIMIC-III CSV dataset and discover it outperforms conventional transfer learning techniques, producing enhancements of up to 139% when compared to the baseline model. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, with the ability to handle a broad selection of classification problems and extracting key data characteristics from wearable devices, such as activity levels and sleep patterns. As a result, FedHealth provides a reliable framework for developing machine learning models in the healthcare field, providing solutions for classification tasks encountered with wearable devices, such as detecting sleep disorders, identifying cardiology events, and forecasting physical activity levels. Consequently, this paper paves the way for the application of transfer learning techniques within the wearable healthcare community, addressing fundamental challenges and showcasing a pioneering approach to developing machine learning models, suitable for real-world healthcare settings, through the FedHealth framework. This paper is a significant contribution to the wearable healthcare domain, presenting a pioneering FedHealth framework that combines federated and transfer learning, along with a comprehensive evaluation, to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. This work has the potential to influence the development of machine learning models in the healthcare domain, by identifying a crucial method for addressing challenges like data privacy, data quality, and classification problems, within real-world healthcare settings. This paper provides a valuable insight into the design of machine learning models, suitable for application in the healthcare domain, also providing a useful perspective on the broader implications of this work, in the healthcare, transportation, and social communities, subject to the compliance with data sharing policies, such as HIPAA, and serving as a starting point for the development of additional architectures, such as FedVision, FedSound, and FedText. This paper is a landmark work on FedHealth, making it eligible for consideration as a premier conference publication, such as a proceedings publication

Researchers in life sciences often collect brief temporal sequences of variable types, including real numbers, categories, and counts, which can be challenging to model and analyze due to their diverse nature and relatively short duration. Conventional machine learning approaches typically prioritize handling long-time series data, common in physical and engineering applications. Each sample data point is usually analyzed separately, with subsequent modeling based on individual features extracted from each time point. In contrast, our proposed monitored learning method, MLTS, seeks to model time series data directly, considering all dimensions simultaneously. By doing so, MLTS can handle a higher number of variables, potentially including genetic expression profiles, without sacrificing performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MLTS by applying it to various time series datasets, including those from Drosophila melanogaster developed by the Katsanis Laboratory at the Johns Hopkins University, and show that it achieves comparable or better results than traditional machine learning methods while significantly outperforming them in terms of computational efficiency. Furthermore, our framework facilitates feature importance visualization, providing a clear insight into genetic regulation across different species. The source code of our implementation, called MonLearn, is now available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/aleksas/monlearn, enabling other researchers to monitor learning on temporal series data. Additionally, there is an accompanying RStudio web application available at https://aleksas.github.io/monlearn/, allowing for easy MLTS parameter selection and visualization of the results. By incorporating a genetic t-cross talk (geneticTC) R-package developed in collaboration with the Johns Hopkins University, MonLearn can handle large datasets, such as 50,000 Drosophila melanogaster expression profiles, within a reasonable time frame. Overall, our monitored learning approach provides a more efficient and effective way to analyze temporal series data in the life sciences, making it a valuable tool for researchers in this field. By utilizing a geneticTC R-package, MonLearn can handle a vast amount of genetic expression data, such as 50,000 Drosophella melanogaster expression profiles, within a feasible time frame. Our analysis revealed a strong correlation between the two CI lines, implying that gas temperature has a significant impact on the observed line ratios. Not accounting for temperature leads to inaccurate estimates of gas density, a potential source of error in previous studies. We are investigating how many past observations are necessary to predict future events in a sequence, especially in sequences that follow a random permutation pattern. This research involves measuring the accuracy of predictions made from a sequence of independent and identically distributed snapshots of the sequence. Our key finding is that, regardless of the number of sequence elements, a small fixed percentage (1/4) of past observations is always sufficient to accurately forecast a large number of future elements. This result is significant because it proves a 1995 conjecture made by Devroye, Györi, and Krug, and the method used to verify it is a useful criterion for evaluating prediction tools. Furthermore, our research also identifies specific conditions under which a smaller percentage of past observations can be used to make precise predictions. Additionally, we explore the application of our findings to the study of unique sequence detection. The main statistical tool used in this research is the Hamming distance metric. 

For the purpose of this abstract, we will use the term "Hamming challenge" to refer to the research issue being investigated. The Hamming distance, which measures the number of different elements between two sequences of the same type, plays a key role in this research. In realistic computer vision applications, identifying and removing shadows is a critical step.  Traditionally, this approach has been modelled using the combination of ambient and direct light volumes.  However, accurately calculating shadows using this method is challenging due to the complex nature of light interaction with obstacles.  In this research, we introduce a novel, distinct, and efficient shadow calculation method based on differentiable volumes.  By utilizing this model, we can leverage optimization techniques and incorporate it into reverse problems, such as disarming shadows in images.  Our system, shadow removal, employs a differentiable shadow calculation method, specifically designed to handle various light sources, materials, and volumes.  Through the use of this model, we successfully remove shadows in images, achieving better results than existing shadow removal techniques.  Our system and model also enable the removal of shadows from videos, something that current techniques cannot accomplish.  One key aspect of our approach is that it allows for light source information to be obtained from images, a capability that other techniques lack.  By utilizing this information, we enhance the performance of our system, especially in video shadow removal applications.  In order to validate our model, we created a dataset consisting of volumetric models and their corresponding shadow images.  This dataset, shadow-100, can be utilized to assess the performance of shadow calculation and removal techniques.  In comparison to state-of-the-art techniques, our proposed method, consistently yields better results, as evidenced by the ranking of our system, system variants, and rival methods in the benchmark rankings.  One key aspect of our approach that sets it apart from other techniques, is the presence of unnatural artifacts in images.  This type of artifacts has a significant impact on computer vision applications that employ image processing operations, such as segmentation.  In order to mitigate this issue, we introduced a novel, efficient, and differentiable model for light interaction with models, specifically designed to handle irregular models.  By utilizing this model, we developed an optimization technique that removes model imperfections, resulting in the creation of models with smooth boundaries.  As a result, the presence of unnatural artifacts in images, is mitigated, leading to the improvement of vision-based actions control, segmentation-based locomotion, and vision-based locomotion applications. The proposed algorithm leverages a dual-layer convolutional neural network (CNN) structure, where the first layer analyzes the video's motion patterns and predicts intermediate frame data, while the second layer refines the prediction based on unique features in each frame. Furthermore, the integration of deep learning algorithms with the DGM enables the development of a cutting-edge, rapid SWE solver that can accurately predict floods in a mere seconds. The concept of "false sense of security" is commonly used to describe a situation where individuals are misled into believing their security risks have been mitigated, when in fact their vulnerability has not changed. It also presents a comprehensive framework for evaluating FSP in various contexts. Specifically, our proposed framework is applied to two well-known cryptographic constructions - the first is an incorrect security proof, and the second is a widely accepted security reduction - as well as to a well-known vulnerability disclosure scenario. Our FSP calculations reveal that users frequently misestimate their security risks, often by an impractically large margin. These findings highlight the utility of FSP in identifying and quantifying the prevalence of false security perceptions. As a result, our proposed framework can inform the design of more effective security awareness campaigns, aimed at accurately communicating security risks to users. This study introduces an innovative approach to establishing converse theorems for Lyapunov functions in the context of control systems that feature unbounded control inputs. Our analysis focuses primarily on the chain of integrators, a prominent class of control affine systems. By leveraging a newly proposed generalised conversation theorem, we demonstrate that a stable equilibrium point existing for a specific system can be associated with a locally defined, smooth Lyapunov function near that equilibrium. This result facilitates the verification of asymptotic stability for systems with unbounded controls, as illustrated through several concrete examples. In particular, this combined method can tackle systems that incorporate sinususoidal terms typically found in the feedback linearisation literature. Overall, our work contributes to the broader exploration of conversational Lyapunov theorems and showcases its applicability to control systems featuring unbounded controls. The new method's advantages are highlighted, and future directions for enhancing its performance are identified. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully created on FPGA, our research strives to take this concept further by integrating a memory system that can efficiently locate and manipulate data in real-time, alongside a set of co-operating processes that can operate on data in parallel. Our execution model allows for both sequential and concurrent program instructions, with a memory system that can handle same-time reads and writes, as well as a mechanism for process competition that can be won or lost. System control is managed through a priority-based scheduler, combined with a match detector that can identify when memory content has changed, facilitating ongoing program execution. Our design includes an in-depth description of the hardware components, as well as a high-level overview of the system's programming aspects. Due to the novelty of this concept, there are currently no existing programs that can be run on this machine, and as such, there are no performance benchmarks to report. Overall, this research lays the groundwork for further exploration into the integration of content-addressable memory and parallel process control in computing systems. With the rapid advancements being made in the development of analog computing technology, our work may provide a potential path towards combining digital and analog elements within a single system. As we continue to push the boundaries of what is possible with content-addressable processing, there are several key issues that merit further investigation, including how to efficiently manage memory interference, develop effective techniques for win/loss strategy, and explore the integration of learning mechanisms that can influence process decision-making. System scalability and how it relates to system scale and number of parallel processes, as well as possible approaches to error detection and correction, are also key areas that require further exploration. With regard to programming techniques, we plan to investigate both manual and automatic methods for generating win/loss strategies, along with the development of higher-level language tools that can efficiently utilize the capabilities of this machine. System-level optimization of code for best performance, as well as the integration of debugging tools that can handle the unique characteristics of this machine, are also key areas that merit further investigation. With regard to potential applications for this machine, we believe that content-addressable parallel process architecture may provide a suitable platform for the development of innovative artificial intelligence systems that can learn from experience and adapt to new situations. We've performed an in-depth analysis of nine galaxies within a $z=2.91$ cluster using Hubble Space Telescope data, yielding high-resolution observations of star formation and accretion activity. These galaxies exhibit compact, rotating disk systems with high-mass galaxies displaying larger scales. European Southern Observatory (ESO) data from FORS2 and VLT allowed us to determine star formation rates, identify the presence of an active galactic nucleus, determine whether a galaxy is interacting, and assess its surrounding environment using the K20S survey. Our findings indicate that galaxies with the highest specific star formation rates typically have the shortest accretion times, while those with the shortest accretion times often have the most extended disks. We propose a three-stage model for the evolution of galaxies: initially, they experience rapid star formation and accretion; later, they enter a phase characterized by controlled star formation and reduced accretion; finally, they undergo a second phase of rapid star formation and accretion, often accompanied by bulge formation and the extension of their disks. This model becomes clearer when considering the relationship between star formation, accretion, and structural changes during the current stage of the galaxy's development, as well as its past and predicted future development. Our analysis of galaxy pairs using the MUSE Spectral Mapping Program has yielded further evidence for our bulge formation model, particularly the link between large-scale interactions and bulge growth. However, we believe that minor mergers and interactions may serve as the primary driver of bulge formation, especially in galaxies with massive central components, rather than massive disks. Our study has initially explored the potential for bulge growth driven by internal processes, especially star formation, and large-scale interactions, especially when considering the full range of galaxy masses, as well as their disk-to-total mass ratios. Our research provides a starting point for a more comprehensive examination of how galaxies form and the role of star formation, accretion, and structural changes in their evolution. Our analysis has led to the following predictions: we expect to detect a larger bulge in galaxies with shorter accretion times and those that have completed their current stage of rapid star formation and accretion; we also anticipate observing larger disks in galaxies with shorter accretion times and those that have entered their next stage of rapid star formation and accretion; our study has further identified potential targets for the MUSE Spectral Mapping Program to determine whether our analysis can be applied to galaxies at different cosmic times, especially when considering how galaxies form

The Texture Zero Flavor (TZF) model, a popular minimalistic model to address the flavor problem, is extensively used in Grand Unified Theories. However, the TZF model's predictions are often verified using ad-hoc methods which may conceal parameter space issues. In this study, a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach is employed to thoroughly assess the TZF model's viability, thereby ensuring a global minimum in the chi-squared function is found. Additionally, the standard matrix ansatz used in the TZF model is relaxed by reintroducing parameters in the neutrino sector, a move justified by the model's minimalistic nature. The MCMC results reveal that the TZF model can only accommodate very small neutrino masses, restricting the accessible parameter space. Moreover, when the standard and relaxed versions of the TZF model are compared, it becomes apparent that the latter can deliver identical outcomes to the latter, albeit at a higher cost in degrees of freedom. The MCMC analysis also identifies the degree of freedom discrepancy in the neutrino sector as the primary obstacle preventing the relaxed TZF model from matching the standard TZF model's performance. Consequently, we propose an alternative, equally plausible, formulation to recover the latter's outcomes, thus revitalizing the relaxed TZF model as a viable theoretical framework. The MCMC employed to evaluate the TZF model can be adapted to assess other low-energy flavor models. The newly devised, high-statistics MCMC interfaces and reconstruction tools, developed to handle the sophisticated neutrino data set that will be generated by the future long-baseline neutrino experiment to be implemented in the Deep Underground Neutrino Archive, are freely available for download at the provided repository link. In the context of the upcoming intense neutrino flux from the Deep Underground Neutrino Archive, the revised relaxed TZF model can serve as a prime target for experimental validation of the neutrino sector. The MCMC analysis yields the necessary predictions for the usual and unusual neutrino observables, as well as the relevant matrix elements, at various energies, which can be used as the TZF model's baseline predictions for the forthcoming experiments. The revised, relaxed TZF model predicts significantly smaller values for the matrix elements than the standard TZF model and, at the highest energy considered, results for the usual neutrino observables that slightly deviate from the MCMC-determined minimum in the chi-squared function. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of categories grows, as it results in a large ambient feature space that can hinder model interpretability. Despite this challenge, various machine learning methods can benefit from a sparsity-promoting approach, such as Group Lasso, to eliminate irrelevant categories and reduce overfitting. However, Group Lasso can struggle to accurately identify groups of highly correlated categorical variables, often due to its conservative estimation of the Lagrange multiplier, which can result in a sparse model that misses crucial information. To address this issue, we present an enhanced Group Lasso solver, called ENHANCE-GL, which uses a more precise estimation of the Lagrange multiplier to better handle such situations, especially when dealing with a large number of groups. When compared to traditional Group Lasso, ENHANCE-GL demonstrates its advantages on both synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its capacity to accurately identify relevant groups, achieve lower prediction errors, and provide more interpretable models. Furthermore, ENHANCE-GL exhibits competitive performance alongside state-of-the-art methods for sparse modeling, such as Group Lasso and Sparsity-inducing Matrix Factorization, while successfully handling extremely large datasets with millions of features. By pairing ENHANCE-GL with a fast Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator, the method can also activate additional features in the model, yielding superior performance. With its user-friendly interface and straightforward implementation, ENHANCE-GL can be integrated with existing software for statistical learning, and its source code is readily available for widespread use. Additionally, an overview of the method's theoretical properties is provided, including support for the consistent estimation of group parameters and model selection, which can be achieved through the use of ENHANCE-GL. With its numerous benefits, we strongly recommend incorporating ENHANCE-GL in the development of sparse and interpretable machine learning models, especially those involving categorical data. Skies are a crucial aspect of landscape images, providing information on weather conditions which can be utilized in photography, meteorology, and various other fields.  Convolutional Neural Networks are frequently employed for weather classification, which relies on extracting features from images to determine the weather.  However, this task is complicated due to several issues such as unpredictable light conditions, diverse backgrounds, and the varied presence of visual elements in images.  In order to improve the classification performance, it's necessary to develop a dataset that includes a broad selection of high-quality images, along with an enhanced data set that addresses the mentioned obstacles.  We introduce the ADE20K-Weather sub-dataset, labeled as AFW, containing 21 categories and comprising 3000 high-quality annotated images, along with an improved data set called AFW-Enhanced, containing 5000 enhanced images.  Furthermore, we conduct thorough evaluations of multiple Convolutional Neural Network models, along with a segment-based approach, on the newly created AFW dataset.  Our research indicates that accurate weather classification depends on multiple factors, including the ability to classify scenes into segments, along with the ability to extract global features from images.  Our results demonstrate that the combination of scene segmentation and global feature extraction plays a crucial role in enhancing the classification performance.  We also observe that the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks can be significantly improved through the use of high-quality training data, along with the incorporation of scene segmentation information.  Our research sets a new standard for evaluating the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks on the AFW dataset, incorporating multiple classes, along with the use of sophisticated segmentation-based approaches.  We anticipate that our AFW-Enhanced dataset, along with our evaluation protocols, will contribute positively to the advancement of advanced image classification techniques.  Our research centered on Convolutional Neural Networks, however, these models are not specifically designed for weather classification, which relies on extracting features from images to determine the weather.  Therefore, we believe that further investigation is necessary to enhance the performance of these models on the AFW dataset.  One potential approach to achieving this could involve the application of Graph Convolutional Networks, which are specifically designed for graph-based data, along with the incorporation of light condition classification, along with the classification of background elements, along with the presence/absence of visual elements.  We are in the process of publishing our research, along with the AFW dataset, which complies with the guidelines provided by the ICLR 2021 dataset

A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. A distinctive feature characterizes the sound produced by an adhesive tape as it sheds: a high-frequency acoustic wave with varying amplitude that persists even after the initial rupture. The pressure within the shed portion increases in response to the short circuit caused by the shedding process. This pressure difference gives rise to the persistent acoustic wave observed in the sound waveform. The persistent wave's amplitude, however, does not match expected values from a simple circuit analysis. Instead, the amplitude varies greatly with different types of shedding. Ultimately, this variability in shedding sounds may be attributed to the persistent acoustic wave's distinct components, which include both a high-frequency wave caused by the pressure increase and a low-frequency envelope resulting from the intershed region's acoustic resonance within the tape. Systematic variations in the persistent wave's amplitude are shown to be influenced by the initial conditions of the shedding process, including the tape's length, its resistance, and the nature of the adhesive used. A numerical model is introduced to illustrate the persistent wave's amplitude's relationship with these factors. This research provides a new theoretical framework for understanding the complex acoustic waves present in shedding sounds and may also offer insights for detecting subtle changes in the shedding process, potentially by analyzing these acoustic waves. A practical detection method is proposed and could be especially useful in identifying slight variations in the tape's length, which is typically difficult to measure directly. This detection approach is then successfully tested with different tape lengths, accurately pinpointing even the smallest changes. Thick-film SQUIDs and planar junctions comprise multiple weak links that severely impede the observation of macroscopic quantum tunneling, whereas single atomic-layer junctions exhibit the desired tunneling phenomenon. This study investigates the critical temperature difference that characterizes the phase-sluggish regime in planar SQUIDs and identifies the optimal design for reviving macroscopic quantum tunneling. Numerical simulation reveals that a square SQUID loop with a very small loop area experiences a critical temperature difference similar to that of a single junction. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that a sufficiently long and narrow loop can be treated as an equivalent series connection of multiple weak links, each corresponding to a section of the SQUID loop. This analysis provides a practical guide for fabricating planar SQUIDs that exhibit macroscopic quantum tunneling. Additionally, we propose a new type of superconducting circuit, based on a wrapped atomic-layer loop, which can serve as an active switch between macroscopic quantum tunneling and coherent single-electron phenomena. This concept offers the potential to create a device that can be programmed to perform either multi-electron tunneling or single-electron coherent operations. This study offers a theoretical framework for designing planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs that can exhibit macroscopic quantum tunneling or single-electron coherent phenomena. Ultimately, our findings verify that the limit model's coefficients match those of the original high-contrast material. We conducted a statistical analysis of enormous early-type galaxies within the KiDS-2000 field using the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam, focusing on tidal features surrounding these galaxies. Our research revealed that the average fraction of light affected by tidal features, or the "tidal fraction," varies significantly based on the mass of the galaxy. Specifically, larger galaxies have a greater tidal fraction, indicating that more massive galaxies are more likely to be affected by tidal interactions. Our study also discovered a correlation between the tidal fraction and the mass of companion galaxies, with higher mass companions causing a greater tidal fraction. Interestingly, we found that the orientation of these tidal features is randomly distributed with respect to the plane of the companion galaxy. By estimating the volume density of companion galaxies, we were able to calculate the merger rate of early-type galaxies. Our results show that one-third of massive early-type galaxies will undergo major mergers within the next 5 billion years. Our study provides insights into the tidal interactions experienced by massive early-type galaxies and may have implications for the growth of massive elliptical galaxies, particularly in the early universe. However, our research also suggests that gas-rich mergers, as opposed to completely non-major mergers, have a significant impact on the development of massive early-type galaxies throughout the universe. Our study may have implications for models predicting the fraction of major mergers contributing to the growth of massive galaxies throughout the universe, with some models, such as the Model by Domínguez and Martínez-Goméz (2019), underestimating this fraction. Our research provides a method for detecting entirely non-major mergers, as opposed to major mergers, which could be applied to multiple datasets, including the SAMUs presented here. Our analysis of the tidal features within the SAGA-COSMOS sample, as opposed to the KiDS-2000 sample, revealed similar statistical patterns, including a correlation between the tidal fraction and the mass of the galaxy. The development of high-power laser systems is a complex process that requires a thorough understanding of multiple technologies. While reference models are available, there is a lack of analysis on enhancing system performance through the optimization of existing components. This work addresses this gap by illustrating the process of improving a high-power laser system using the example of a solar-pumped laser, specifically a solar-pumped CO2 laser system. We employed mathematical modeling to analyze the performance of a conventional planar solar concentrator and a new design featuring a cylindrical refractive solar collector. The simulation showed that the cylindrical collector can increase the collected power by a factor of 4.8 and reduce the required solar concentration ratio by half. The improvement in the solar collector is attributed to the increased collection efficiency of the cylindrical collector, which is 21.4%, compared to the conventional planar collector's 4.5%. The enhanced solar collector can collect up to 43.8 kW of power using a solar concentrator with a 1 m2 aperture and a concentration ratio of 100, potentially pumping up to 9 GW of CO2 laser power. The design of the cylindrical collector provides a pathway for optimizing the performance of various laser systems. Furthermore, this work demonstrates the applicability of reverse engineering to the development of high-power laser systems, addressing concerns related to the potential for misuse. With the advent of inexpensive computer-aided design software and 3D printing technology, there is a risk that illicit fabrication of high-power laser systems could compromise national security. To mitigate this threat, it is essential to analyze and disclose the design of such systems, along with their components, to prevent the creation of devices with unintended consequences. The development of a solar-pumped CO2 laser system using a cylindrical collector is an open path for other researchers to follow, highlighting the necessity of transparent disclosure in the scientific community. This work is a solution to this challenge, allowing researchers to explore the design of various high-power laser systems. The described methodology can be applied to the design and analysis of numerous laser systems, enabling the development of new solar-pumped laser systems through open disclosure and potential collaborations. With this approach, the scientific community can prevent the unauthorized fabrication of dangerous devices and instead create innovative, beneficial technologies. The documentation of the design of a solar-pumped CO2 laser system using a cylindrical collector and 3D printing technology is available on the iGUBS website. As modern Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) experiments employ increasingly complex and sophisticated instruments to achieve higher sensitivity, it has become essential to validate observations using careful simulations that account for instrumental characteristics. However, developing and maintaining separate tools for instrument modeling and post-processing analysis can be challenging for research groups. To address this issue, we have created an open-source Python package called s4cmb, which provides a unified framework for simulating CMB experiments, post-processing map analyses, and data visualization. s4cmb enables users to input parameters for CMB skies, filter functions, and instrumental characteristics to generate simulated data. It then uses this information to calculate key figures of merit, such as noise levels, pixel covariance matrices, and window functions. By providing a comprehensive and customizable modeling of CMB experiments, s4cmb aims to facilitate a clear understanding of instrumental biases and limitations, and to provide a valuable tool for analyzing current and future CMB experiments. To showcase its capabilities, s4cmb has been applied to the CMB experiments CMB-S4 and BICEP/Keck II. Leveraging open-source code and contributing to the public CMB code repository, we have released s4cmb on the GitHub platform for the benefit of the CMB community. Through its user-friendly interface and extensive documentation, s4cmb is designed to be an intuitive tool for researchers to model CMB experiments and associated foreground components. By using Python, which is widely used in the CMB research community, s4cmb can easily integrate with popular analysis tools and libraries, such as Numpy, Scipy, and PyCMB. To facilitate collaboration and knowledge exchange, we have established an issues forum on the GitHub s4cmb website, where users can share their questions, provide feedback, and suggest new features for the package. To the knowledge of the authors, s4cmb is the first open-source Python tool that offers a comprehensive post-processing analysis framework for CMB experiments, featuring a sophisticated modeling of instrumental biases and foreground components, and is the first package to model the BICEP/Keck II experiment. Additionally, we have released publicly available Python notebooks on the GitHub s4cmb website, which provide clear instructions on using s4cmb and incorporating its features into popular Jupyter notebooks used for teaching CMB courses. Recent studies using pre-trained language models for word arrangement tasks have shown significant advancements. It has been observed that these models can achieve high accuracy levels without utilizing any specific arrangement techniques. This research aims to explore the underlying capabilities of pre-trained language models to perform such tasks by examining the results of an experiment featuring the BART model. Word pairs with both compatible and incompatible meanings were created and the model's ability to distinguish between them was analyzed. The research found that the BART model is capable of identifying word pairs with incompatible meanings that have similar syntax but cannot differentiate between words with incompatible meanings that have varying syntactical structures. For a given number field $K$ of degree $n$, we establish limits on the values of successive minima of ranks in number fields. Specifically, we show that for any non-hypotenuse prime $\mathfrak{p}$ in $K$, the sequence of ranks at $\mathfrak{P}$ division ranks for forms associated with $\mathfrak{p}$-adic embeddings has a maximum of $n$ distinct values. We also investigate the potential for such a sequence to reach $n+1$ or more ranks at a given prime, which could imply the existence of infinitely many $\mathbb{Q}$-curves in certain situations. Notably, if we find a set of binary forms with ranks reaching the maximum of $n$ or $n+1$ at a prime $\mathfrak{P}$, we can use them to construct an $\mathbb{Q}$-curve with $n$ or $n+1$ $\mathfrak{P}$-places of bad reduction, respectively. Our current results improve upon their findings by removing the requirement on places of bad reduction being non-hypotenuse and set the stage for future works to explore the generalised successive minima of ranks in number fields. A significant eruption, with an exceptionally large ejection volume, occurred on April 12, 1985, at the dwarf nova AD Leo.  Despite extensive study of this event, researchers have yet to agree on a unified explanation.  Analysts have typically modeled the extreme white light flux observed during the eruption's initial stage using conventional residual gas dynamics while accounting for the disk's partial coverage as seen from Earth.  However, these conventional models fail to accurately account for the eruption's massive ejection volume as seen in ultraviolet spectra, which show a superposed structure during the main stage of the eruption.  A new study presents an alternative explanation, proposing that the eruption's visible continuum was overridden by a massive hot disk flare until around 1000 UTC on April 12.  Utilizing this idea, together with updated observations and earlier data, the team of researchers has developed a new set of simulations to better understand the eruption's development over time.  Their models suggest that multiple components, including the disk's edge, the ejected gas, and the disk flare, all merged around 1000 UTC, resulting in a temporary resurgence in the observed white light flux.  This new analysis provides a more comprehensive view of the eruption, further supported by UV spectra that show the same sequence of events, and highlights the importance of considering all spectral bands simultaneously in the analysis of such events.  This study's findings may also imply a causal link between the massive flare and the extensive gas ejected during this dwarf nova's huge eruption.  Researchers have further demonstrated that both optical and ultraviolet spectra obtained during this event are consistent with a scenario in which the massive gas eruption was caused by a massive hot disk flare, and with models that accurately predict the flare's behavior over time.  Lastly, this study's strategies for analyzing and modeling such events may be useful for interpreting recent observations of another well-known dwarf nova called OT Ser. Systems similar to AD Leo provide valuable opportunities to study the internal physics of soft X-ray transient binaries that contain accretion disks.  Therefore, further research into the physics of these systems is crucial and will become even more important as even more sensitive instruments, such as the SEEDS instrument on the Jupiter II, are capable of detecting even smaller outbursts from these objects.  This study's findings may also contribute to the broader understanding of how massive flares can lead to the extensive gas eruptions commonly seen in soft X-ray transient binaries and provide a more comprehensive view of the internal physics of these binary systems. This investigation into the behavior of PT-symmetric waveguide networks reveals their capacity for transmitting waves, achieving perfect transmission, and experiencing coherent absorption-lasing. Our analysis highlights the relationship between these phenomena and the notion of bidirectional clarity, which is well-demonstrated through numerical simulations using a finite difference method. The complexity of PT symmetry in these systems leads us to define a new metric called the bidirectional clarity index, which quantifies this property. The PT phase of a waveguide network is indicated by the presence of a gap in its transmission spectrum, and its location determines whether the wave's transmission exhibits left-right, right-left, or no symmetry. Notably, coherent absorption-lasing and perfect transmission are observable in PT-symmetric systems, and they can also occur in systems with a high bidirectional clarity index. However, our research reveals that this property is a hallmark of PT-symmetric systems, and it cannot be solely defined by the presence of a symmetry-induced gap in the transmission spectrum. Furthermore, we propose a concept called flawless transmission, which is characterized by the absence of transmission clearance in PT-symmetric systems. This distinction enables PT-symmetric systems with a gap in their transmission spectrum to be classified as either exhibiting clear transmission, absorption-lasing, or flawless transmission, depending on the index of their central unit cell. Finally, our analysis extends to PT-symmetric dimers, where we find that the phenomenon of transmission clearance, absorption-lasing, and flawless transmission are all dependent on the dimer's configuration and unit cell indices. Additionally, we discover that a PT-symmetric dimer can emulate a PT-symmetric trimer by adjusting its mirror symmetry, and that this operation transfers its capacity for transmission clearance, absorption-lasing, and flawless transmission to the dimer. The interplay of these phenomena with bidirectional clarity and the index of the central unit cell, however, cannot be replicated by a dimer. Our investigation provides a foundation for further research into the behavior of PT-symmetric waveguide networks and the development of PT-symmetric photonic systems that utilize transmission, absorption, and emission in a coordinated manner. By doing so, we aim to create a more versatile approach that can easily adapt to a wide range of temporal scenarios. To support this, our model uses two separate but interconnected graphs - one for temporal information and another for event types. Our research indicates that this hybrid approach not only results in more accurate event timestamp predictions but also enables the identification of potentially erroneous or unknown events. Furthermore, our model's time-aggregation capability allows it to efficiently process a large quantity of temporal data. Our work's effectiveness is demonstrated through both offline and online evaluation, confirming the benefits of our approach over traditional time-aware models. By applying our methodology to real-world events following a non-linear timeline, we also achieve superior performance compared to other knowledge graph methods. Our research paves the way for the exploration of non-linear time-based models and the development of more accurate event timestamp predictors, such as those with high-rank, stochastic, and dynamic temporal relations. These location data can provide detailed information on individual behavior, spatial population distribution, and carrying capacity, which are crucial for parameter estimation in capture-recapture studies. However, current capture-recapture models often disregard location data, relying solely on recapture information to estimate population parameters. This paper proposes a new multi-state capture-recapture model that incorporates location data, which can be in the form of encounter history or resource choice data. This model utilizes location data to estimate capture probabilities, accounting for factors such as habituation at capture sites and individual preferences for specific locations. This results in more accurate population parameter estimates, including capture probabilities, population size, and density. Our research demonstrates that capture-recapture models incorporating location data through resource choice logs yield more precise estimates than traditional capture-recapture models. Furthermore, this study showcases the utility of capture-recapture models that utilize location data through choice logs, which can be achieved using the RMark package in R. By leveraging a mix of neural networks and symbolic manipulation, this framework can accurately identify the structure of forms, detect key components such as text fields and buttons, and extract the data entered into these fields. The issue of polarization has gained significant attention over the recent past, particularly within Western democracies, where it has led to rising discontent among voters and eventually contributed to various social and political crises. To tackle this challenge effectively, it's crucial to have a clear, standardized framework for measuring polarization, especially one that distinguishes it from noise and data anomalies. This study compares the effectiveness of widely adopted indicators of polarization, such as the average distance between agents, the variation in opinions among agents, and the dispersion of opinions around the political spectrum, in different scenarios. To test their validity, these indices were applied to both artificial and real-world data, including datasets from European Parliament elections and a literature review of US research. The results show that the most reliable methods for measuring polarization are those that consider the distribution of opinions, particularly in response to external factors that can mask polarization, such as sampling errors, ballot probing, and measurement tools with limited scale. To address this issue, a new approach called Multi-Instructor Labeled Data (MILD) has been proposed, which involves multiple human instructors providing partial labels for a single data point. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian whose evolution gradient accurately represents the target function, and a problem Hamiltonian whose ground state reflects the desired equilibrium state. To minimize complications, quantum annealing protocols are often designed using stoquastic Hamiltonians whose zero-field ground state is orthogonal to the desired equilibrium state, and this process is typically facilitated by periodic driver Hamiltonian transformations. However, we demonstrate that this seemingly convenient setup can lead to catastrophic convergence failures when coupled with decoherence, a universal phenomenon affecting quantum systems, especially when non-stoquastic driver Hamiltonians are used. To counter this, we present an alternative and universally applicable quantum annealing algorithm, first refined for the case of classical noise, and subsequently proven theoretically that it surpasses the pitfalls of conventional approaches. Furthermore, our experiment using a quantum annealing processor in the presence of two-level quantum noise supports our theory's validity. This work provides a groundbreaking solution to the long-standing challenge of quantum annealing, and our findings are highly relevant to the development of practical quantum systems for optimizing complex functions. To overcome the difficulties associated with quantum annealing, we demonstrate an unfeasible transformation for converting an arbitrary Hamiltonian into a stoquastic form, and present a scenario in which a customer-specific quantum processor is constructed to achieve the optimal outcome. Additionally, we introduce a new protocol known as the decoherence-compensated quantum annealing algorithm, and apply this innovation to the example mentioned earlier, resulting in a profound improvement in the success probability by a factor of approximately 10^10. This groundbreaking progress was independently verified using two distinct simulation methodologies. Moreover, we explore the possibility of enhancing the drive strength in the presence of decoherence, and successfully implement this compensation technique on our superconducting quantum annealing processor, achieving a staggering improvement in the success probability by a factor of approximately 10^5. This impressive outcome was independently validated using two distinct simulation methodologies. Building on this achievement, we introduce the universal protocol known as the decoherence-compensated continuous-time quantum annealing algorithm, and successfully demonstrate its efficacy on our superconducting quantum annealing processor, thereby breaking through the persistent barrier that has hindered the development of practical quantum systems for optimizing complex functions. This breakthrough, where the degree of the drive Hamiltonian exceeds that of the target function by a significant margin, represents a major breakthrough in quantum processing

We investigate left-invariant actions of groups on trees, focusing particularly on those generated by a set of edges whose associated graph has no cycles. Notably, we prove that such groups possess local group action properties equivalent to those guaranteed by the graph quotient method, established by Tits. Moreover, we establish that these groups are precisely those whose action on a tree for which they are transitive, combined with some additional technical conditions, allows us to define a left-invariant ordering compatible with the group's action. As a result, we demonstrate that groups generated by a set of edges whose associated graph has no cycles are equivalent to groups obtained from Coxeter systems. Finally, we prove that the property of having a left-invariant, graph-based ordering is a subgroup property of these groups, yielding numerous subgroup lattices with interesting properties. Additionally, this property is shared by twisted groups derived from 2-generator free groups whose graph has no cycles. We explore potential connections between these results and the broader theory of graph groups. Moreover, we identify potential research directions and open questions within this field.

Large-scale quantum computing relies on coding techniques to counteract quantum error syndromes that occur during computation. This paper introduces an original approach to developing coding codes using reinforcement learning, specifically code production 'learners'. These learners use computational resources, possibly affected by errors, to create encoded versions of computational modules 'atoms'. The code learners operate in an automated environment where their coding decisions minimize the likelihood of computational failures. We utilize a simple qubit example to illustrate this failure-resilient coding concept. Investigations into code learner performance reveal that their coding abilities can rival those of optimized quantum error correction codes, especially when the atomic failure rates are very low. However, when the failure rates are higher, the code learners may need a significantly larger code to achieve the same level of failure reduction. This research provides an initial exploration into combining fault-tolerant quantum computation and reinforcement learning. It also raises questions about how code learners might deal with noisy quantum environments, as well as potential applications in scheduling coding operations and optimizing code parallel processing. These issues are discussed along with future direction suggestions. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/ghshent/qrqc. The code learners described in this paper assume a specific quantum architecture, namely the surface architecture, but the approach is likely applicable to other quantum hardware as well. The code learning framework may also be applied to other fault-tolerant quantum applications that involve encoding computational modules.
