In educational settings, curiosity is both a driver of personal growth and a crucial skill, yet it can be challenging to maintain due to various obstacles.  From a neurological perspective, curiosity is associated with the brain's default mode network and the anticipation of pleasing outcomes.  As students work in groups to learn, their curiosity may be sparked by each other's ideas, fueling an interest in exploration and engagement with the subject matter.  To better understand how curiosity develops and is maintained in group learning settings, we developed a unique multimodal method that combines verbal and nonverbal behavioral analysis with physiological feedback.  By utilizing this method, we gathered data on how primary school students' curiosity changed over time in a collaborative learning environment.  Our results showed that certain variables such as gender and prior knowledge had a significant impact on initial curiosity levels, while variables such as ethnicity and previous experience had a more substantial impact on how curiosity evolved over time.  Additionally, our findings revealed that students with higher curiosity levels tended to exhibit a more active learning approach, while those with lower curiosity levels tended to exhibit a more passive approach.  Our novel multimodal design provides a framework for further research into the complex factors that influence curiosity in educational settings, and we believe that this type of research can contribute to the development of more effective learning materials and teaching methods.  By using this method, we were also able to create an innovative assessment tool that can be used to evaluate the curiosity levels of learners in educational settings.  This study was conducted as part of the European Commission's H2020 program, and the data collected is available for download from the Open Science Framework platform.  We have also created an interactive 3D visualization of the learning environment used in this study, and this can be accessed through the Unity Game Engine.  Overall, our unique approach to investigating curiosity in group learning settings has shown promising results, and we are confident that it has the potential to be a valuable resource for any future studies in this area. The development of neural network-based models, specifically those employing attention in multiple forms, has led to significant advancements in natural language processing tasks. However, the reliability of these models has raised critical concerns, given their widespread adoption in high-stakes applications, including but not limited to remote education, healthcare, and financial interactions. Unfortunately, the field of attention-based models lacks a clear understanding of the implications of gradient sensitivity, particularly in contexts where attacks from crafted inputs can compromise both the model and the user interacting with it. This study aims to illuminate the underlying issues related to the sensitivity of attention-based models and highlight the shortcomings of current evaluation methodologies. We introduce a novel metric, called layer-wise maximum aggregate gradient (L MAG), designed to provide a comprehensive assessment of a model's sensitivity. Furthermore, we introduce a new type of attack called average activation attack (AAA), which serves as a benchmark to evaluate the efficacy of defense strategies. The results of our research are publicly available on both GitHub and ArXiv, where we have released the implementation details of both the AAA attack and the L MAG metric. We strongly advise the use of L MAG in conjunction with existing evaluation methods such as gradient penalty (GP) and layer-wise gradient penalty (LGP) to ensure the robustness of attention-based models. We also urge researchers and practitioners to consider incorporating AAA into their testing protocols to validate a model's security before deploying it in real-world settings. Additionally, we have provided guidance on the effective use of both L MAG and AAA, including recommended threshold values, along with detailed analysis of both the theoretical and practical aspects of these methods. We believe that the integration of L MAG and AAA into the standard evaluation pipeline for attention-based models will serve as a crucial step in assessing their reliability and potential vulnerabilities before integrating them into high-stakes applications. We have also explored the application of both L MAG and AAA to transformer-based classifiers and encoder-decoder models, demonstrating the versatility of these methods in evaluating the robustness of a wide range of attention-based models. We have identified key limitations in the capability of both defense algorithms and attack methods to handle the complexity of certain input data, such as the challenges associated with parsing human language, which provide valuable insights for guiding the development of future research. To understand this concept, it's helpful to first analyze the simpler case of a standard Brownian motion. For a standard Brownian motion, the square of the global persistence is directly proportional to the local duration, with this relationship holding true for large numbers of n. As we deviate from this basic case by introducing obstacles into the walk, we need to reevaluate this relationship. This study uses independent and non-trivial results to determine how the global persistence relates to the local duration for a wide range of stochastic walks, including those with loops of varying sizes and those without loops at all. Depending on the specific characteristics of the walk, the local duration may be proportional to n to the power of -1 with a negative coefficient, this relationship being a fundamental property of the walk itself, or it could be affected by additional factors such as the walk's probability of making a mistake, the size of its steps, or the type of environment it's walking in. This study provides a clear and detailed explanation of the underlying principles, while also offering a summary of the variables that can be used to describe the global persistence. This study uses a pay-per-use method to break down the walk's duration into two distinct components: the time spent walking in a single direction and the time spent switching direction. We demonstrate W-Net's effectiveness by applying the network to the TU-ABDOMEN dataset, achieving a significant improvement in nucleus identification accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Our work builds upon the previous achievements of Art LeClair and Freydoon Shahidi in this context. Specifically, we demonstrate that SO(2r+1)(E) or Sp(2r+1)(E) possesses enough irreducible smooth E-representations that are fully made up of the absolutely recurrent components with respect to the absolute global norm on the Adele ring of E. Our work is a key contribution to the regional converse theorem for these groups. Furthermore, this achievement has significant implications for the Bessel functions and the non-vanishing of certain automorphic L-functions. In 1975, Basu established an interesting result which shows that under certain conditions, a statistic t(n) is an unbiased estimator of a parameter theta, if and only if t(n) is a function of the complete and sufficient statistic for theta. We explore extensions of this result, examining nontransitive relationships between Basu's conditions and the concept of a minimal sufficient statistic. Our findings illustrate how likelihoods can lead to circular relationships, resulting in which condition can imply another, depending on the specific context. Therefore, we propose the term "nontransitive likelihoods" to describe situations in which Basu's framework exhibits cyclic dependencies, in contrast to the more familiar concept of nontransitive relations which involves a direct contrast between distinct elements. Finally, we highlight how the property of nontransitive likelihoods can yield intriguing, though ultimately insignificant, differences in the behavior of Bayes factors and the likelihood ratio test. In the process, we identify a useful but previously unrecognized consequence of Basu's theorem, which we call the "Basu's Legacy Property". This property ensures that the renowned result continues to hold considerable value even in the face of circular relationships between its conditions. Recent successes in dialog comprehension tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods emphasizing contrastive learning during dialog pre-training. Nonetheless, numerous dialog comprehension dialogues contain little or no explicit annotations. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured semi-supervised pre-trained model for dialog comprehension. It utilizes a novel tree-structured contrasting pre-training approach to leverage unlabelled dialogues to learn representations. This model includes three main components: a contrastive loss function that extracts pairs of related or unrelated documents from a dataset, a graphical encoder that combines pre-trained word embeddings and encodes the document as a graph, and a decoder that generates a document embedding from the graph. By doing so, SPACE-2 is capable of processing documents of any length and can be applied to various dialog comprehension tasks. Experimental results show that SPACE-2 achieves exceptional performance on key dialog comprehension tasks, including dialog classification, role recognition, and text-to-speech. The model excels particularly in situations with limited annotated data. Additionally, it demonstrates versatility in multi-domain settings. This paper formulates three spheres theorems for functions subject to the Dirac equation using the principles of Clifford analysis. We establish three separate theorems, each corresponding to a variant of the classic Cauchy-Kovrijkina theorem, and demonstrate the interrelation between these results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an alternative approach to these theorems is achievable via the application of the Fejer-Jackson theorem within the context of Clifford analysis. Additionally, this paper introduces the concept of a spherical function in the context of Clifford analysis, along with its implications. We define a monogenic function as being spherical if it is expressible as the sum of a harmonic polynomial and a monogenic polynomial, and we establish the interrelation between these spherical functions and the three spheres theorems. We also demonstrate that the application of the Dirac operator to a spherical function yields another spherical function. This line of reasoning provides a new framework for understanding the three spheres theorems. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. Developing effective parts-of-speech tools for Arabic requires a significant amount of annotated data, which can be challenging to achieve due to the language's complexities, particularly when it comes to distributing annotation tasks among human resources. To tackle this issue, we've designed a user-friendly web-based platform called MADARi, which enables the efficient annotation of Arabic texts for parts-of-speech and spelling corrections through a collaborative approach. By utilizing state-of-the-art user-friendly interfaces and incorporating tools like a morphological analyzer and a search engine, MADARi makes annotation easier and more manageable for non-experts, including native Arabic speakers. The platform's user-friendly interface and integrated features also facilitate the detection of anomalies in annotated data, which can be pinpointed and re-annotated by the community. To demonstrate the efficacy of MADARi, we've conducted a usability study and incorporated a significant corpus of annotated data, including the Arabic Web Pages Corpus, which we believe can serve as a resource for training machine learning models. The MADARi platform is available online at https://madari.seas.uottawa.ca/. To the best of our knowledge, MADARi is the first publicly accessible web-based platform for collaborative Arabic morphological annotation and spelling adjustments developed with modern web technologies. By providing a user-friendly interface and an intuitive annotation tool, MADARi addresses the issue of annotating Arabic texts through community effort and opens up opportunities for conducting a free, open-label community study. Additionally, the study's design and results are presented and an analysis of the collected data is provided. Furthermore, MADARi has been successfully used in the context of a university course, which showed promising results and highlighted the potential of integrating the platform into educational programs. To facilitate the reproduction of the study, the MADARi system, including its annotation tool and user interface, is made available for research purposes at https://github.com/amir-h-ma/madari. By providing a state-of-the-art, open-source implementation of a community-based annotation platform, we aim to contribute to the development of advanced natural language processing tools for the Arabic language. While computer-assisted polyp analysis has shown potential, the current challenge lies in its limited training data, which hinders significant progress. To address this issue, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive collection of colorectal polyp histopathology images tagged with adenoma abnormalities and classification information obtained from leading international repositories, including the Chair Pathology Society (CPS) and partially derived from the Medpedia database. Our dataset, which has been made publicly available, comprises 14,299 images (24,038 regions of interest) annotated for adenoma classification and characterization and outperforms existing collections. To facilitate future advancements in computer-aided polyp analysis, we've also established a benchmark to evaluate and compare classification and characterization models, using which we achieved notable results with a conventional convolutional neural network (CNN). performed better on ViI-D than ViI-N. To overcome the difficulty of large vocabulary 
sizes, we explore the application of natural language generation techniques,
